sections.heading: AasthiChain
sections.text:
Own premium Indian real estate from ₹500

 Fractional property tokens on an append-only ledger · atomic delivery-versus-payment · UPI money leg 

 
 
 
 

Live site · Ledger explorer · Settlement rail · Calculators · Learn

</div 

---

A premium flat costs ₹75 lakh and you cannot buy 0.1% of it. AasthiChain converts a registrar-verified
property into a fixed number of tokens (a ₹75 L villa becomes 15,000 tokens at ₹500 ) and settles
the money leg and the ownership leg as one atomic operation. Both move, or neither does.

 Stack: a Go settlement core, a Node API edge, a React frontend, and Hyperledger Fabric chaincode.

 Honest scoping. The settlement rail is a faithful simulation . There is no public UMI API and
 no live NPCI credential outside a bank partnership; real access is the SEBI Regulatory Sandbox.
 Every simulated surface is labelled as such in the UI and in API responses. What is real: the
 ledger, the atomicity, the verification rules and the guardrails. The exact line between the two
 is itemised at the end of this file.

 Contents : Quick start · How it fits together · Pages · What you can do · Settlement rails · On a real Drunix network · Guarantees · Testing

Deeper reading: Architecture and internals · Testing · Audit · Contributing

sections.heading: What you can do
sections.text:
Buy a fraction. Browse the marketplace, open a property, buy from ₹500. Payment and ownership
settle together: a buyer who cannot pay gets nothing and the seller keeps every token. Before money
moves, the app asks the rail whether the trade would settle, so a shortfall is a sentence rather
than a failure discovered afterwards.

 Check that a listing is real. Every property page answers, in plain language: was title validated
by a registrar, and who (an owner validating their own listing is refused outright); is the deed
fingerprinted, and does it collide with another listing; does the ledger still replay cleanly. You
can prove your own copy of a deed matches the ledger without uploading anything: hash it locally and
paste the result.

 Ask the assistant. A question box answers how things work and what is listed. It gets the same
public listing data a visitor can already see and nothing else: asked who holds what, it refuses and
points at the public ledger. Asked about a property that does not exist, it says so. It has no way to
move a token, a rupee or a document.

 Hold many properties as one unit. A basket is a single tradeable unit backed by a fixed recipe
of several properties. Creating one moves the underlying tokens into custody, which is what makes the
unit redeemable rather than notional. A basket that is not fully backed is never allowed to look
healthy.

sections.heading: What you can do (continued)
sections.text:
Earn rent, split fairly. Rent and coupons are paid straight into holders' wallets. The split can
follow a snapshot of who holds what today, or how long each holder actually held , so someone who
bought yesterday does not collect a full quarter's rent.

 Know the address is a real one. When a property is listed, its pincode is checked against the
national postal directory and the answer is kept with the listing: confirmed, in a different place
from the one claimed, or not a pincode anybody posts to. The check is a courtesy and not a
gatekeeper, so an unreachable directory records that nothing was checked rather than inventing a
pass, and it never pretends to be proof of ownership. This is one of the few boundaries the platform
declares as genuinely live.

 Withdraw a listing and have it stay withdrawn. A withdrawal is recorded against the property
rather than quietly dropped, so it survives a restart and holds across every view, and asking twice
is not an error. Anyone still holding tokens is bought out at the listed price first: the tokens
return to the owner and the payout is written to the ledger, because taking a listing off the market
must not strand the people who funded it.

 See the whole history. Ownership is a journal of changes, not just a balance, so the register can
be replayed for any window.

sections.heading: Settlement rails
sections.text:
ASI, the Aasthi Settlement Interface

In September 2026 SEBI and RBI launched Demat 2.0 : bonds issued as native tokens on the
depositories' permissioned DLT, with the cash leg settled in wholesale CBDC (e₹-W) through the
Unified Market Interface, with ₹1,025 crore issued by REC, L&T and IIFL. AasthiChain already had both
ends. This is the middle.

 ASI is our own rail, built to that pattern , not a connection to the real UMI, which is reachable
only through a bank partnership or the SEBI sandbox. What follows is implemented here, end to end,
and can be run and audited from this repository.

- Atomic DvP. Both legs move or neither does; a failure leaves no half-settled state.
- Central bank money is conserved. Balances always reconcile against lifetime funding, so the rail
 can neither create money nor destroy it.
- Programmable servicing. Rent and coupons paid pro-rata on the due date, no registrar file
 exchange.
- Safe retries. A repeated settlement request returns the original outcome instead of settling
 twice, and a failure stays a failure.
- Standards trace. Every instruction carries the ISO 20022 message family a real
 securities-settlement rail would emit.

Refusals are always specific: which side was short, and by how much. Never a generic error.

 Work orders: upkeep paid on delivery

sections.heading: Settlement rails (continued)
sections.text:
A tokenised building still has to be inspected, repaired and revalued, and that cost used to sit
outside the model: off-ledger, on trust, against an invoice nobody could audit. The fee is
 reserved on the funder's e₹-W wallet when the order is funded (reserved money cannot be spent on
anything else, including a settlement), and moves to the worker in the same locked step that anchors
the deliverable's SHA-256 to the ledger. There is no state in which someone has been paid and no
evidence exists.

Only the funder pays out, only the assigned worker can deliver, and a dispute freezes the escrow
rather than deciding anything. Whoever supplies the worker sits behind an adapter, which runs as a
simulation: no external provider is integrated. Design notes:
 docs/WORK ORDERS.md .

sections.heading: Anchored on a public blockchain
sections.text:
The settlement ledger here is permissioned, which is the right shape for settlement and also the
obvious objection: replaying it proves it agrees with itself, not that it is the history that
existed yesterday. So the head of the chain is published to a public blockchain as a digest, and
after that, rewriting history would mean rewriting a record on a network nobody here controls.

What crosses over is one line: the chain id, the block height, the block hash and the transaction
root. No participant, no asset, no amount. An anchor proves a digest existed at a time; it does not
claim the contents behind it are true, and the settlement data never leaves the service.

This part is not a simulation. The network calls are live, the transaction format is the real one,
and verification works for anyone with no account and no funds. Publishing costs a fee, so it stays
switched off, and says so, until a funded key is configured: docs/ANCHORING.md .

sections.heading: Central bank money on the ledger
sections.text:
The settlement asset here is a simulated digital rupee, and it lives on the chain rather than in a
table beside it. Money is issued by the central bank role, moves between accounts, and is redeemed
back; every paise issued is either in an account or has been destroyed, and that arithmetic is
published for anyone to check.

Three behaviours follow the pilot rather than the brochure. Money can be bound to a purpose, with
an expiry, a merchant category, named merchants and a geography, so a food subsidy can only be
spent at a fair price shop and a spend outside the rule is refused on the rail instead of
reconciled later. Value can be carried offline as a signed voucher for places connectivity does
not reach, with small limits and a double spend that is caught on reconnection rather than hoped
against. And money can be locked against an event, so a cancelled flight pays its own refund the
moment the airline attests the cancellation: no claim, no form, no wait.

Every movement records two different things that are usually said as one. Technical finality is
the block being committed, which takes milliseconds and happens around the clock. Financial
finality is the payment being irrevocable, which in central bank money is the same moment, and
over a commercial bank rail is not. Where the two differ this layer says so and names the window:
 docs/CBDC.md .

sections.heading: Cross-border, as five different things
sections.text:
Sending money abroad is not one rail. A scheme-to-scheme link, an aggregator, a correspondent bank
chain, a card network and two central bank ledgers settling against each other differ in who may
carry the payment, how much may move and how long somebody is exposed in the middle. Each is
modelled on its own terms here, and a payment is refused by the corridor that cannot carry it,
with the missing authorisation named rather than hidden behind a generic error.

The difference that matters is whether both legs sit on the same ledger. When they do, settlement
is atomic: one movement, no interval in which one side has paid and the other has not. When they
do not, the gap is real, and it is closed either by a hash time-locked exchange where revealing
the secret completes both sides or by a confirmation from the institution on the far side. Until
that happens the payment is reported as provisional, with the window named:
 docs/CORRIDORS.md .

sections.heading: A model that was trained, not a rule sheet called AI
sections.text:
Payments are screened by hand-written rules: amount bands, velocity, a structuring window. Those
rules are honest and they are not machine learning, so they are no longer described as if they
were.

Alongside them runs a classifier that was actually fitted in this repository, on a labelled
dataset, with its coefficients committed and its accuracy measured on data it never saw rather
than asserted in a sentence. It held an AUC of 0.824 and caught about seven in ten of the
fraudulent payments in the held-out split, at roughly six in ten precision.

Two things about it are stated everywhere it appears. The training data is synthetic, because no
one hands a project like this real labelled fraud, so the score describes the generator and not
the world. And it is advisory: the published rules make the decision, the model is reported beside
them, and where the two disagree the disagreement is shown. Every score comes back with the
features that moved it: docs/RISK MODEL.md .

sections.heading: Money that can pay money of a different kind
sections.text:
A digital rupee that can only pay another digital rupee wallet is a closed loop, which is why
pilots stay pilots. Here the shopkeeper keeps the QR code they already have and the payer chooses
what to pay with, and the interesting part is what that costs rather than that it works.

Three questions get separate answers instead of being averaged into the word instant. Which leg is
final and when: paying a bank account is final on this ledger immediately and provisional on the
bank side until the scheme settles, and it says so rather than showing a tick. Who holds the claim
in between: a named suspense account whose balance is published, because the gap always has
somebody in it. And whether the total changed: swapping a bank claim for central bank money is one
operation that destroys one and creates the other, with the conservation check returned alongside.

Pulling money out of a bank account is listed as not supported, with the reason, because that needs
a connection and an authorisation this deployment does not have. Recording that the far scheme
settled is a person's act and the ledger names them: docs/CBDC.md .

sections.heading: Verification that produces the tier, instead of trusting it
sections.text:
A wallet's KYC tier used to be a word in the request that opened it, which made every ceiling built
on that tier a rule enforced faithfully against a fact nobody had checked. It is now the output of
a verification: a route, evidence kept as a hash, an expiry, and a trail.

Which route is used decides what follows, exactly as the rules intend. Identification over a video
call with an official, a liveness check, the PAN shown on the call and the holder in India is
treated as equal to meeting somebody, and carries no ceiling for being remote; miss any one of
those and it is refused with the list of what was missing. A one-time-password route is permitted
but capped at a lakh a year with closer scrutiny, because nobody met anybody. An offline identity
file goes stale after three working days. Records expire on a schedule set by risk band.

The part worth stating plainly: this system refuses to hold an Aadhaar number. Submit one in any
field and the request is rejected rather than quietly redacted, because the compliant pattern for
anyone without a licensed vault is not to receive it at all. What is kept is the reference the
offline route returns, which carries only the last four digits, and even that is hashed before it
reaches a block. The verification steps themselves are simulated and say so on every response:
 docs/KYC.md .

sections.heading: An agent that proposes and never acts
sections.text:
The useful half of an agent in a settlement system is noticing. The dangerous half is acting. This
one keeps the first and refuses the second: it reads live state, drafts a specific action with the
evidence that prompted it, and stops. A correspondent leg outstanding past its window, a
conditional payment hours from expiring with nobody having attested, a screening case nobody has
picked up, backing that has gone stale: each becomes a drafted action in a queue, with its reasons,
what approving it would do, and what happens if it is ignored.

Nothing it drafts runs on a timer. A named person approves, and at that moment the facts behind the
proposal are read again: if the world moved while the proposal sat there, it goes stale and nothing
is performed. The ledger records the approver, not the agent, because "the agent did it" is not an
audit trail.

It also does not choose its own actions. Noticing is ordinary code reading ordinary state, and the
short list of things an approval can cause is published by the system rather than described in
documentation. It cannot create or move money, cannot close a compliance case, cannot attest to
anything, and cannot approve its own work: docs/AI AGENT.md .

sections.heading: How much of this is actually tested
sections.text:
A pass count is not a coverage figure. Ninety-nine suites passing says nothing about how much of
the settlement rail they reach, so there is a tool that measures it: it maps every action the rail
exposes, replays each suite against that map without running anything, and marks each action as
certainly covered, possibly covered, or reached by nothing. Same commit, same number, on any
machine.

The current answer is 58.1% of 86 actions certainly covered , with another 18.6% possible and
the rest untouched. That figure is published because it is unflattering and because a number
nobody recomputes is a claim rather than a measurement: a check in the suite fails if the published
figure drifts from the measured one, or if coverage falls.

It paid for itself on the first run by showing that moving and redeeming digital rupees were
exercised by nothing at all, while the identity those two paths can break was being asserted
confidently. There is also a small harness that plants realistic defects, a threshold nudged out
of reach, a guard dropped, to check the suite notices. Four of five were caught; the fifth was not,
and chasing it turned up a real hole in the approval logic as well as in the tests. Both are fixed:
 docs/TESTING.md .

The approach is lifted from Scapia's write-up of their Argus test lab, which published its own
uncomfortable coverage numbers rather than its pass rate.

sections.heading: How fast, measured rather than claimed
sections.text:
On the two-core container used for development, settlement runs at about 37,900 nanoseconds of
engine time per settlement : roughly 26,000 a second in a tight loop, with a median of 0.027 ms
and a 99th percentile of 0.131 ms. Over HTTP, with requests arriving one at a time, the same box
served 25 settlements at a median of 0.17 ms and a 99th percentile of 0.252 ms.

Two caveats that matter more than the figures. The contended benchmark barely differs from the
serial one because the box has two cores, so at most two things were ever really running: that is
not evidence the design scales, only that there was not enough parallelism available to find out.
And the lock wait is zero because nothing ever queued, which means under that load the engine was
not the constraint. The live page shows what this process has actually served, and says "nothing
measured yet" when it has served nothing.

sections.heading: How fast, measured rather than claimed (continued)
sections.text:
That figure describes delivery versus payment and nothing else, so the other money paths are now
timed separately rather than borrowing it. A corridor eligibility check costs about 400
nanoseconds because it deliberately moves nothing; creating central bank money about 21,000; a
digital rupee transfer about 46,000, which is more than a settlement because it runs a screening
pass and screening is the expensive part. Completions and refusals are counted apart, since a
refusal returns before the work it refused: docs/THROUGHPUT.md .

sections.heading: Screening that is a list, a case and a report
sections.text:
Checking a payment against sanctions and politically exposed person lists used to be a sentence in
a document here. It is now three things that can be exercised. Names are matched against a loaded
list in a way that survives the usual evasions: a missing full stop, a different transliteration, a
dropped middle name, an honorific. A strong match stops the payment before it moves; a resemblance
lets it go and opens a case, because a similar name is a question rather than an answer, and both
thresholds are published rather than buried.

A hit then becomes a case file somebody has to work: picked up, annotated, and either cleared with
stated grounds against the reviewer's name or escalated. Escalation produces an actual document,
with the subject, the transaction, the grounds and a narrative, hashed so the copy held and the
copy produced can be shown to be the same one.

Two things are said everywhere this appears. The list shipped here is synthetic, because publishing
a copy of a real sanctions list in a demonstration invites somebody to rely on it and a stale list
is worse than none; a deployment with a licensed list configures its own and the screening says
which is loaded. And nothing produced here is filed with any authority: the report is an artefact,
not a submission: docs/AML.md .

sections.heading: An assistant that answers from this project, not from memory
sections.text:
The assistant on the site is grounded in two things, and neither of them is what a language model
happens to recall about blockchains. The first is this project's own documentation: every design
document is indexed and the sections that match a question are put in front of the model as
written, with the document they came from, so an answer can be traced back to a file anyone can
open. The matching is plain word scoring rather than an embedding service, which means the same
question retrieves the same passages on every deployment and costs nothing to run.

The second is the rail as it stands at the moment of asking: how much digital rupee is outstanding,
whether supply still conserves, which cross-border corridors refuse payments here and which
authorisation each one lacks, and the measured metrics of the trained model with the fact that its
training data was synthetic attached. Those figures are used as given; the model is not allowed to
recompute or round them.

sections.heading: An assistant that answers from this project, not from memory (continued)
sections.text:
It can also now answer about one specific thing. When a question names a reference, a settlement, a
block, a conditional payment, a cross-border transfer, that record is fetched and answered from. The
model is not handed a tool to go and get it: the reference is recognised and the record is fetched
by ordinary code, so naming a settlement can only ever cause a settlement to be read. A reference
that matches nothing is reported as matching nothing.

When no source covers a question the assistant says it is not documented and points somewhere
useful, which is the whole point: it still reads only, still cannot act, and is switched off
entirely where no key is configured: docs/AI AGENT.md .

sections.heading: Paying from outside India
sections.text:
Tokens are easy to send across a border; the consideration for Indian property is not. The law
requires it to arrive in rupees through banking channels, and a foreign national of non-Indian
origin resident outside India cannot buy here whatever they pay with. So the cross-border leg does
the only thing that is lawful: the stablecoin is received and converted outside India, and the
buyer's rupee wallet is credited only against an attestation that an inward remittance landed, with
a bank advice reference and a purpose code behind it. Eligibility and the transfer-information
rules are checked before a quote is given, and a refusal is recorded as plainly as an approval.

It is a simulation, labelled as one: no chain is connected, no custody is held and no money moves.
The screen for it is linked from the home page, and asking as a buyer who is not allowed to purchase
shows the refusal rather than hiding the option. The reasoning, the sources and what it deliberately
does not claim: docs/CROSS BORDER.md .

 Money leg: UPI Collect

sections.heading: Paying from outside India (continued)
sections.text:
A payment is a lifecycle, not a hop: requested, approved, released, reconciled, with every amount held as
an exact figure, so no rupee is lost to arithmetic. The round-trip runs against a real provider's
test environment, so signed requests and callbacks are validated by the provider rather than graded
by us. Each payment is risk-screened before approval, and the screen explains its reasoning rather
than returning a score. No real money moves.

---

sections.heading: On a real Drunix network
sections.text:
The settlement core runs in simulation by default, and the hosted demo is simulating. The chaincode,
though, has been deployed to a real NPCI Drunix network, which is NPCI's Hyperledger Fabric fork,
and written to.

On a two-organisation Drunix test network, a property registration submitted through the gateway
was endorsed by both organisations, ordered, and committed. The gateway reported the peer-assigned
transaction id and block number, and the committing peer, which runs none of this repository's
code, reported the same chain head independently.

Getting there took three fixes, and all three were invisible to a single-peer test. Two were real
defects in this chaincode: values that differed between endorsing peers, so no write could ever
agree with itself, and index entries in a format the network's state database rejects, which took
the peers down rather than the transaction. The third was in the test network's own tooling. Each
is now guarded by a test, and each is written up with its symptom, repro and fix in
 docs/DRUNIX.md and docs/REPOSITORY AUDIT.md .

What this claims: the chaincode and the gateway work against Drunix. What it does not: the hosted
demo is not connected to a Drunix network, /trust says so, and nothing here is an NPCI endorsement
or a pilot participation.

---

sections.heading: Guarantees
sections.text:
The record is append-only and survives restart. An entry is written durably before the change it
describes is treated as real. Once written it is never erased, and each entry is sealed against the
one before it, so an altered history announces itself instead of passing quietly.

 Supply is scarce. Tokens cannot exceed a property's authorised supply, and an owner's unsold
stock is never counted as allocated.

 Issuance cannot outrun stated backing. Where somebody accountable has stated how much of an
asset exists, with evidence and a date it must be refreshed by, issuing past that figure is refused
and the refusal is written down. A statement past its refresh date stops authorising anything. The
platform checks the arithmetic, not whether the statement is true, and says so.

 Holder identity is private. A visitor sees how many people hold a property and in what
proportions, under anonymous labels. Real names need a session, so the marketplace stays open to
browse without leaking a cap table.

 Approval is independent. Title validation is restricted to a Registrar, and refused when the
validating identity registered the property.

sections.heading: Guarantees (continued)
sections.text:
Your things answer only to you. Being signed in is not being entitled: your wallet, payments,
holdings, documents and notifications are yours, and a stranger is refused even knowing the
reference. A regulator can look where that is genuinely the regulator's job, and nowhere else.

 A reference is not a key. A bank reference on a receipt proves the payment happened. It reveals
nothing about who else was involved.

 A pause means paused. A supervisor's halt is written down before the answer comes back, so it
survives a restart and applies to every route that could move those tokens. A longer way round is
not a way round. The same authority can lift it; both halt and lift are permanent record.

 Withdrawal does not strand a holder. A listing cannot leave the market while someone still holds
it without that holder being bought out in the same step, and both the withdrawal and the payout are
permanent record.

 Nothing reaches the record around the rules. Every ownership change passes the same approvals
whichever way it is attempted.

 A refusal is never a dead end. If the record stops verifying, the platform stops rather than
building on history it cannot vouch for, and there is a supervised way back that writes down what
was set aside, why, and on whose authority. It has been used once, and the record of it is still
there to read.

---

sections.heading: Testing
sections.text:
A mass failure is almost always a dead rail rather than a bug, so check the core is up first. CI
runs the Go modules separately, builds the frontend, and treats formatting as a hard gate.

Some defects no suite here can reach: three were found only by deploying to a real two-org network,
and each now has a regression test. Exact commands, prerequisites, expected output and the
deliberate gaps: docs/TESTING.md . A verified list of current weak points:
 docs/REPOSITORY AUDIT.md .

sections.heading: Contributing
sections.text:
Issues and pull requests are welcome.

1. Fork, branch from main .
2. Keep money rules in the settlement core. A rule added to the edge will be asked to move.
3. Run make test and make test-go before opening a PR. gofmt is a hard gate in CI.
4. The API exists in two implementations that must stay in step; see docs/ARCHITECTURE.md .
5. New behaviour ships with a test that fails without it.

Commit messages are plain language describing the why , not a changelog of the diff.

The full guide, including the design rule that gets pull requests sent back and a list of genuine
starter tasks, is in CONTRIBUTING.md . Participation is covered by
 CODE OF CONDUCT.md .

Found a security flaw? Please report it privately: see SECURITY.md .

<details 
<summary <b What is live vs simulated</b (click to expand)</summary 

 Live and real: the ownership rules and their duplicate-deed guard, the append-only record, atomic
settlement and its rollback, safe retries under concurrency, conservation of money, independent title
validation, verified sign-in, the supervisory halt and the way back from it, and durable storage. The
assistant is live, and its limits (public data only, no ability to act) are enforced on the server
rather than requested of the model.

sections.heading: Contributing (continued)
sections.text:
Simulated, and labelled as such: the national payments rail (no live credentials exist outside a
bank partnership), the wholesale CBDC wallets (e₹-W is an RBI pilot, not a public API), the UMI rail
itself (real access is the SEBI Regulatory Sandbox), government-issued KYC, the land-record lookup,
and the public-chain escrow experiment.

 The payment round-trip is genuinely real as far as it goes: the provider's test environment
accepts our signed requests, and tampered amounts and bad signatures are rejected by them, not by us.
Only the settlement behind it is simulated.

</details 

<details 
<summary <b Regulatory context</b (click to expand)</summary 

The Asset Tokenisation (Regulation) Bill 2026 is a pending Private Member's Bill, not law. It
proposes KYC/AML obligations, a registered custodian, registrar validation and a regulator freeze
power. AasthiChain maps to all four: a Registrar org validates title, a Regulator org can freeze, the
cap table is auditable end to end, and the payment path enforces a KYC gate.

 SPV structure. Real platforms wrap each property in a special-purpose vehicle, so a token is a
beneficial interest in the SPV holding legal title (Registration Act 1908 + the 2026 Bill). That is a
legal structure, not a code change, and is documented as Phase 2 rather than built.

</details

sections.heading: The problem
sections.text:
The mandate layer already answers "what is this agent allowed to do, on whose behalf, under what
limit, until when". That is the authority half, and it is the half most of the industry is still
missing: the EU wallet framework verifies the principal to the hilt and says almost nothing about a
piece of software presenting a bounded grant of someone else's authority.

What it does not answer is the accountability half. Today a mandate names its principal in the
clear on a public ledger. That is one of three architectures a jurisdiction can pick:

1. User-sovereign. The principal holds credentials and discloses selectively. Strong against
 overreach, but accountability depends on the principal cooperating, and per-transaction consent
 does not scale to software making thousands of decisions.
2. State-escrow. Identity withheld from commercial counterparties and held by government,
 released by legal process. Accountability does not depend on cooperation, at the cost of
 concentrating a re-identification capability in one place.
3. Cryptographic threshold. Opening the pseudonym requires several independent parties to
 cooperate, enforced mathematically rather than institutionally. Best abuse resistance, hardest
 to operate.

Naming the principal in the clear is none of these. It is the counterparty-sees-everything default,
which is the one option nobody is arguing for.

sections.heading: What is built here
sections.text:
The third architecture, with the trigger and the record borrowed from the second.

- An agent acts under a pseudonym : agent:aasthi:<hash . Counterparties see the pseudonym, the
 agent's stated purpose, and the fact that a liable principal stands behind it. They do not see
 who.
- The principal is split across named custodians with Shamir's secret sharing over GF(256). Any
 k of n custodians can reconstruct it; k - 1 learn nothing at all, which is a property of
 the scheme rather than a promise of good behaviour.
- Opening the pseudonym is a governed event, not a lookup . Somebody opens a request with a
 stated trigger, custodians contribute shares one at a time, and the identity is reconstructed
 only when the threshold is reached.
- Every step is a block : the request, each approval, and the reveal itself. A principal can
 never be un-masked quietly, and the record of who asked, who agreed and why outlives the people
 involved. A request that nobody completes expires and stays on the chain as an unanswered ask.
- The passport binds to the agent's purpose and version label and to its mandate, so the
 question "which exact software acted" has an answer separate from "who answers for it".

sections.heading: What it is not
sections.text:
- The custody is simulated. All shares live in one process on one host. The protocol is real
 (the arithmetic genuinely requires k shares) but the distribution is not: a host operator has
 every share. Real deployment means one share per organisation, held by that organisation. The
 API says this in the response rather than in a footnote.
- It is not anonymity. The pseudonym is re-identifiable by design, so under the data-protection
 reading that applies here it remains personal data and must be treated as such. The claim is
 accountable pseudonymity, nothing stronger.
- No zero-knowledge proof of principal attributes. The sponsorship fact is asserted by the rail
 from its own participant register, not proved to a third party cryptographically.
- It does not make the agent legal. Which legal person answers for an agent is a question of
 law. This records an answer and makes it recoverable; it does not create one.

sections.heading: Rules
sections.text:
- Only the principal registers an agent, and a participant may not register itself as its own
 agent.
- Custodians must be distinct, at least two, and the threshold must be at least two and no greater
 than the number of custodians. A threshold of one is refused: that is the state-escrow model with
 the safeguards removed.
- Only a named custodian may contribute a share, and only once per request.
- A revoked passport still reveals. Revocation stops the agent acting; it does not erase who was
 accountable for what it already did.
- The reveal returns the principal to the requester and writes the principal into the block. An
 opened identity is opened in public, because a quiet reveal is a worse failure than no reveal.

sections.heading: Why this matters beyond the demo
sections.text:
Cross-border recognition is the stated endgame for agent identity, and it will favour whoever built
to an open, inspectable pattern. The pattern here is deliberately boring: a pseudonym, a bounded
mandate, a threshold escrow, and an append-only record of every time the escrow was opened. None of
it is novel cryptography. The novelty, such as it is, is that all four are in one rail and every
one of them is checkable by somebody who does not trust the operator.

sections.heading: The question
sections.text:
Can Aasthi AI become an agent, or a "perfect model" for real estate?

Short answer: an agent, yes, and this repository is unusually well placed to build one. A perfect
model, no, and chasing one is the wrong spend. The two paths are different projects and only one
of them pays off here.

sections.heading: Why not a model
sections.text:
The evidence against training or fine-tuning a real estate model as the headline feature:

- REAL (arXiv 2507.03477), the only serious benchmark for housing transactions and services, built
 from 5,316 expert-checked entries: the best public model averages about 50 percent on its
 multiple-choice topics, and every model tested scores below 50 percent on reasoning. When a query
 contains a fictional place name, hallucination runs 61 to 93 percent, against under 6 percent
 when the entity is real. A model asked about a property that does not exist invents it.
- Where LLMs do measurably help valuation, they help as a feature extractor, not as the valuer. On
 9,842 Oslo transactions, LLM-extracted features fed into XGBoost cut valuation RMSE from 10.53 to
 7.97 percent. The gradient-boosted model stayed the model. Separate work finds LLMs systematically
 overconfident on price intervals and weak on spatial and temporal reasoning.
- Retrieval beats training for this class of problem. Reported reductions in hallucination from
 grounding a model in retrieved source documents run 70 to 90 percent, and the 2026 enterprise
 default is retrieval first, prompting second, fine-tuning only for format or style.

sections.heading: Why not a model (continued)
sections.text:
So: no fine-tune, no in-house valuation model, no "Aasthi AI estimates this flat is worth X". What
is worth building is the retrieval and tool layer underneath, because that is where the accuracy
actually comes from.

sections.heading: Why an agent, and why here
sections.text:
The repeated finding across 2026 industry reporting is that agentic real estate fails on data, not
on intelligence. McKinsey's framing is the "factual layer": property, unit, lease and vendor records
that the agent treats as ground truth, which in practice live in spreadsheets, undigitised PDFs and
systems that do not talk to each other. When that layer is wrong, an agent does not make a small
mistake, it executes a confident wrong action at speed. A second thread says the missing piece is
infrastructure rather than models: listing systems do not expose permissioned, machine-callable
interfaces, so an agent has nowhere safe to act.

AasthiChain already is that missing layer, for its own scope:
 What an agent needs What the rail already has 
 --- --- 
 A factual layer that cannot be quietly edited An append-only chain, replayable and restart-durable 
 Evidence that a claim was made by somebody accountable Signed credentials, attestation accountability, and now proof of backing 
 Bounded authority to act Agent mandates: named actions, expiry, spend counted on the ledger 
 A way to pay only on a verified result The outcome layer: acceptance criteria, escrow, verification, dispute window 
 An audit trail of what the agent did Every consequential action commits a block

sections.heading: Why an agent, and why here (continued)
sections.text:
That combination is exactly what the external agent-payment work is converging on: a signed,
scoped authorisation from a human (Google's AP2 mandates, now with the FIDO Alliance) sitting above
whatever rail moves the money, with a hard rule that irreversible actions pause for a person. The
mandate layer here predates that reading and matches its shape. The gap is not authority, it is
that nothing currently drives it except a human clicking.

sections.heading: What Aasthi AI is today
sections.text:
A read-only assistant. It is given public listing data, never session or holder data, it computes
every number in deterministic code and asks the model only to phrase it, it makes no tool calls and
has no write path, and it is off entirely when no key is configured. That is the correct starting
point and none of it should be relaxed.

Its limitation is also exact: it cannot answer "which of these assets is actually backed", "what
happened in settlement 4f2a", or "show me every attestation this registrar withdrew", because it
cannot look anything up. It only knows what was stuffed into its prompt.

sections.heading: Grounding: documents and live state, not recollection
sections.text:
Shipped. The assistant now answers from two sources besides the listing view, and both carry a
provenance the reader can check.

 The project's own documentation. Every document in docs/ , plus the README, is split into
sections by heading and committed as a retrieval index. A question is scored against those sections
with BM25: lexical, deterministic, no embedding call, no vector database and no network hop, so the
same question retrieves the same sections on every deployment and a wrong answer can be traced to
the section that produced it. The top sections go into the prompt as written, with the file they
came from, and the rules tell the model to prefer them over anything it remembers, to name the
document when it uses one, and never to cite a document it was not given. Notes to ourselves are
excluded: a backlog, an open-problem audit and a deployment runbook are not statements of fact, and
an assistant quoting a to-do list is worse than one that says it does not know.

sections.heading: Grounding: documents and live state, not recollection (continued)
sections.text:
The rail as it stands right now. At question time the deployment reads its own rail: how much
digital rupee is issued and outstanding, whether the conservation check passes, how many corridors
are configured, which ones refuse payments here and exactly which authorisation each one lacks, and
the measured metrics of the trained risk model together with the fact that its training data was
synthetic. These are the rail's own figures. The model is told to use them as given and forbidden to
recompute, round or extrapolate them.

 When neither covers the question , the prompt says so explicitly and instructs the assistant to
answer that it is not documented here and point at the likeliest page. A refusal with a direction is
a complete answer; a plausible guess is not. Retrieval returns nothing at all when the question
shares too few words with anything written down, which is what keeps an unrelated question from
dragging in the least irrelevant section available.

sections.heading: Grounding: documents and live state, not recollection (continued)
sections.text:
A named record, fetched by reference. Summary state answers "how much is outstanding"; it does
not answer "what happened in settlement UMI-3F2A9C1B04", which is the question people actually
arrive with. References in a question are now recognised by pattern (settlement instructions,
tokenised assets, digital rupee conditions, movements and grants, cross-border transfers, and a
block by its height), the matching records are fetched by this code, and the facts go into the
prompt. The model is given no tool to call: a model that chooses its own endpoint is a model that
can be talked into choosing one, and this sits in front of a settlement rail. A settlement id can
only ever cause a settlement to be read. At most four references are followed per question, only
public records are reachable, and a reference that matches nothing comes back as "no record exists
with that reference", which the prompt requires be passed on as written.

Nothing about the read-only promise changed: still no tool calls, still no write path, still off
entirely when no key is set.

sections.heading: The design: a proposing agent, not an acting one
sections.text:
Three tiers, with the boundary between them enforced in code rather than in the prompt.

 Tier 1, grounded reads. Give the assistant a small set of read-only tools over the rail: asset
and coverage lookup, ledger search, settlement status, attestation history, credential
verification, portfolio summary for the caller's own identity. Every tool is scoped by the caller's
identity header, so the agent can never read more than the person asking could read. Answers cite
the block or the record they came from, and the agent is required to say "not in the record"
rather than guess. This is the entire accuracy story, and it is most of the value.

 Tier 2, proposals. The agent may draft an action but never perform it: a settlement
instruction, a work order with acceptance criteria, a backing refresh reminder, a reconciliation
query. It returns a signed-off-by-nobody proposal object that the UI renders with its arguments
visible, and a person approves it. The MCP specification's own guidance is the rule to copy here:
reads can run freely, anything irreversible, money-moving, permission-changing or outbound pauses
for a human who can see the exact arguments before dispatch.

sections.heading: The design: a proposing agent, not an acting one (continued)
sections.text:
Tier 3, mandated execution. Only once Tier 2 is boring. An approved proposal executes under an
existing agent mandate: named action, expiry, spend ceiling, every use counted on the ledger. No
new authority mechanism is needed, which is the point of having built the mandate layer first. An
agent without a valid mandate gets the same refusal any other caller gets.

A useful property of staging it this way: Tier 1 is independently valuable, and if Tier 2 never
ships, nothing is half-built.

 Tier 2 as built

Tier 2 now exists, and it is narrower than the sketch above in one deliberate way: the model does
not choose the action. Detection is ordinary code reading ordinary state, and each detector can
emit exactly one kind of proposal with arguments taken from the record that triggered it. A model
that picks its own action can be argued into picking one, and this sits in front of money. Where a
language model is configured at all, its job is to explain a proposal that already exists.

sections.heading: The design: a proposing agent, not an acting one (continued)
sections.text:
Four detectors, each watching for a situation where the right next step needs a person:
 What it notices What it drafts 
 --- --- 
 A correspondent leg outstanding beyond its stated five-day window Chase the far institution and record their confirmation 
 A conditional payment inside six hours of its deadline, unattested Flag it for attention: it will not release or extend 
 An AML case open for a day with no reviewer Flag it for attention: it will not clear or report 
 Backing gone stale or over-issued Ask the named attestor for a current statement 

Three rules make the queue safe to work from:

 Approval re-reads the world. A proposal carries the facts it was drafted from. When somebody
approves it, those facts are tested again. If the transfer was already confirmed, or the case
already picked up, the proposal goes stale and nothing runs. An approval is permission to act on
the state that justified it, not on whatever state exists later.

 The approver is the signed caller, never a field in the request body. An approval that can name
somebody else is not an approval. The block records the person; "the agent did it" is a sentence
this layer never produces.

sections.heading: The design: a proposing agent, not an acting one (continued)
sections.text:
The whole list of effects is four handlers , and two of them only write a record. The agent
cannot issue, redeem or move money, cannot clear or report an AML case, cannot create an
attestation, cannot approve its own proposal, and never runs on a timer. Those limits are published
by the layer itself rather than described here, so they can be checked rather than trusted.

The queue is public even though deciding is supervisor-only: a list of drafted actions that only
its operator can see is a list nobody can hold to account.

sections.heading: Honest scope: what it must refuse
sections.text:
- No price estimates, no yield projections, no "good investment" judgements. The platform does not
 publish an AVM and the agent must not become one by accident.
- No statements about people or neighbourhoods. Describe the property, never the likely buyer.
- No claim that an attestation is true. The rail checks arithmetic, not reality, and the agent
 inherits that limit word for word.
- No reading of another participant's holdings, KYC, payment details or private collection values,
 enforced by the identity header rather than by instruction.
- No invented record. If a lookup returns nothing, the answer is that nothing was found.

sections.heading: India-specific constraints that shape the build
sections.text:
- A listing card is an advertisement under RERA section 11(2), so any text the agent generates
 about a project has to carry the registration number and must not state possession dates, carpet
 area or amenities that differ from the filing. Practically: generated copy is drafted, never
 published, and anything factual comes from the record rather than the model.
- The DPDP Act treats a chatbot operator as a data fiduciary. Rules were notified 13 Nov 2025,
 consent-manager obligations land 13 Nov 2026, the substantive duties 13 May 2027. What that means
 for this build: notice before the conversation, itemised description of what is processed, a
 retention and deletion path for transcripts and any embeddings, masked logs, and a named
 processor relationship with whatever model provider is called. The two highest-risk gaps named in
 the field guidance are prompt injection and unmasked personal data sent to the provider.
- Prompt injection deserves its own line. The moment the agent reads attacker-influenced text, a
 listing description or an uploaded document, that text can try to steer a tool call. Tier 1 and
 the identity scoping contain the blast radius, which is a further argument for not giving the
 model write tools.

sections.heading: Evaluation, because "it felt good" is not a result
sections.text:
Before any of this is called working, a fixed question set with known answers drawn from the seeded
demo data, run as a suite like everything else here:

- grounded answer rate: every factual claim traceable to a record the tools returned
- abstention: does it say "not in the record" when the record is empty, measured with deliberately
 fictional asset ids, which is the REAL benchmark's exact failure mode
- scope: zero leakage of another identity's data across the whole set
- refusal: valuation, advice and demographic prompts refused
- proposal correctness: generated instructions validate against the rail's own schema

A number from that suite is publishable. A demo transcript is not.

sections.heading: Order of work
sections.text:
1. Tool layer plus identity scoping, read-only, with the evaluation suite written alongside it.
 Built differently: grounding is injected by server code (documents, live rail state and
 records named by reference) rather than exposed as tools the model may call, for the same
 reason the proposing agent does not choose its own action.
2. Citations in the UI: each answer shows the blocks and records behind it.
3. Proposals with human approval, arguments visible, nothing dispatched without a click. Built. 
4. An MCP server exposing the same read tools, so external agents can use the rail as the factual
 layer. This is the piece the rest of the industry is missing and the cheapest differentiator
 available here.
5. Mandated execution, only after 3 and 4 have been boring for a while.

sections.heading: What this is not
sections.text:
Not a deal-sourcing pipeline, not lead generation, not voice, not a CRM assistant. Those are real
products and other people are building them. The thing only this repository can offer is an
assistant whose every answer is backed by a record that a third party can verify independently.

sections.heading: The honest summary
sections.text:
The CBDC half and the cross-border half are both built now, and every keyword
raised has code behind it. What is left is depth rather than absence. Speed is
now measured per path rather than only for DvP, so the remaining partials are
led by the older modules that still keep their state in Go maps while writing
blocks about it (items 8 and 20), which is the one that would take real work.

Two rows were added on 22 October 2026. Item 26 came from an incident rather
than a question: eight certificate authority private keys turned out to be
small integers, so the same question was asked of this rail and the answer
was uncomfortable enough to fix the same day. Item 27 is a requirement rather
than a gap being excused: the tokens are real positions in the Go ledger and
a public contract would let a holder prove one without asking us.

sections.heading: Why not Solidity, and why not Python
sections.text:
A fair question, and the answer is different for each.

 Solidity. Solidity is the language of the EVM, and the EVM is only worth
paying for when the thing being built needs a public permissionless chain with
untrusted participants. The system here is a market infrastructure: the
participants are a registrar, an issuer, a regulator and identified investors,
settlement is in central bank money, and the rules are regulatory rather than
economic. Putting that on an EVM would mean paying gas per settlement, holding
a key for each participant, exposing an order book to the public mempool, and
accepting an execution environment where reversing a mistake needs a migration.
The regulator's own wholesale pilots do not run on public EVMs either.

Where a public chain genuinely helps, the project already uses one rather than
pretending a private ledger is the same thing: the head of the chain is
anchored to Solana, with the transaction encoding written by hand and
verification open to anyone. That buys the one property a permissioned ledger
cannot give itself, which is proof it was not rewritten. There is also a
read-only EVM mirror on Sepolia for document anchors.

sections.heading: Why not Solidity, and why not Python (continued)
sections.text:
So the honest position is: Solidity is the right tool when the trust model is
"nobody", and the wrong tool when the trust model is "a regulator and named
institutions". Writing a contract in it to look blockchain-native would be the
same mistake as calling a rule sheet AI.

If you want it anyway, the defensible version is narrow: a small Solidity
contract on a testnet that holds the anchor digests and the condition rules,
so an outside party can verify a release without trusting this rail. That is a
day of work and I can do it, but it should be built because it adds
verifiability, not because the word is expected.

 Python. Python is the right language for training and nothing in this
repository argues otherwise. The reason the trainer is in Go is narrower than
a preference: training and inference must compute features identically, and
the cheapest guarantee of that is one function called by both. A Python
trainer would need the feature extractor reimplemented, which is the single
most common way a model silently stops working in production.

sections.heading: Why not Solidity, and why not Python (continued)
sections.text:
That reasoning stops holding the moment the model stops being a logistic
regression. Gradient boosting, sequence models over payment history, or
anything needing scikit-learn, PyTorch or pandas should be trained in Python,
exported (ONNX or plain weights), and run in Go behind the same interface,
with a conformance test asserting the two implementations of the feature
vector agree row for row. That is the point at which the language should
change, and it is a real one, not a concession.

sections.heading: What was wrong with what was here before
sections.text:
Payments were scored for fraud and a reporting threshold was applied, and that was described as
AML. It was not. Three things were missing, and they are the three things the work actually
consists of.

 A list. Sanctions and politically exposed person screening is a name-matching problem against a
published list. A system with no list is not screening; it is asserting. And the matching is hard in
exactly the ways that matter: transliteration (Volkanov, Volkanoff), word order, dropped middle
names, honorifics, company suffixes.

 A case. A hit is not a decision. Somebody picks it up, writes down what they concluded and why,
and either clears it or escalates it. An alert with no case file behind it cannot be audited and
cannot be defended.

 A report. The output of an escalation is a suspicious transaction report: a structured document
naming the subject, the transaction, the grounds for suspicion and whoever filed it. Until that
artefact exists, "we report suspicious activity" is a sentence rather than a capability.

sections.heading: How matching works
sections.text:
Names are normalised first: lowercased, punctuation removed, honorifics dropped ( Mr , Shri ,
 Dr ), whitespace collapsed. Each name is then compared as a bag of tokens against the primary name
and every alias on each list entry. Every token of the shorter name is paired with its best partner
in the longer one by edit distance, and the result is scaled by how much of the longer name was
covered, so a lone surname cannot score as a hit against a full name.

Two thresholds, published on the status endpoint rather than buried:
 Similarity What happens 
 --- --- 
 0.93 and above The payment stops. A case opens. 
 0.80 to 0.93 The payment continues and a case opens, because a resemblance is a question rather than an answer. 
 Below 0.80 Clear, and the response still names the list it cleared against. 

Blocking at 0.85 would stop every payment to anybody sharing a surname with a listed person, which
is how screening gets switched off in practice. Letting a near match through unexamined is the
opposite failure. The two thresholds exist so that neither is necessary.

Every match carries its score and a plain sentence explaining it ("2 of 3 name parts matched
exactly; overall similarity 0.94"). A reviewer who cannot see why something matched cannot judge
whether it should have.

sections.heading: The list
sections.text:
The list shipped in this repository is synthetic . Every name in it is invented. Publishing a
copy of a real sanctions list inside a demonstration project invites somebody to rely on it, and a
stale sanctions list is worse than none at all. Every surface that touches screening says which
list is loaded and whether it is the synthetic one.

A deployment holding a licensed copy of a real list points AML WATCHLIST PATH at it. The format is
the same: name, aliases, kind ( SANCTION or PEP ), programme, country, source. Nothing else
changes, and the status endpoint then reports the list as configured rather than synthetic.

The list is readable by anybody. A person refused by a screen is entitled to know what they were
screened against, and a list nobody can read cannot be corrected.

sections.heading: The case file
sections.text:
A case records the screening that caused it, the payment it relates to, and every step since, each
one timestamped and attributed:

 

Clearing a case requires stated grounds; "cleared" with no reason recorded is exactly what an audit
finds and cannot explain. A cleared case cannot be reported afterwards, and a reported case cannot
be cleared: reopening a settled question means opening a new case, which leaves the first decision
visible rather than editing it away.

Cases and reports are supervisor-only, because they carry names and allegations. The list and the
thresholds are public.

sections.heading: The report
sections.text:
Escalation produces a document: subject, counterparty, amount, the related payment reference, the
stated grounds, the matches that triggered it, and a narrative. It is hashed with SHA-256 and the
hash is committed to the ledger, so the copy somebody holds and the copy that was produced can be
shown to be the same one. The response says how to check it: recompute the hash over the document
with its hash field emptied, and compare it to the block.

The document says, in its own text, that it has not been filed with the Financial Intelligence Unit
or any other authority, because it has not. This project files nothing with anybody.

sections.heading: Where it bites
sections.text:
Cross-border transfers screen the originator and the beneficiary before anything moves. Those are
the names the Travel Rule already requires above the threshold, so there is nothing extra to
collect. A listed beneficiary is refused with ERR UMI AML BLOCKED , which is deliberately a
different code from a corridor refusal: the two have entirely different remedies. A near match lets
the payment go and leaves a case open before it lands, which is what a bank actually does.

sections.heading: What this is not
sections.text:
It is not a compliance programme. There is no customer risk rating, no transaction monitoring
typology library, no ongoing screening of existing customers against list updates, and no
regulatory filing. The screening is name-only: no date of birth, no identity document, no
secondary-identifier scoring, all of which a real screening system uses to cut false positives.
Nothing here is a regulatory determination, and the list designates nobody.

sections.heading: The problem it solves
sections.text:
The settlement ledger is permissioned and this process controls it. Replaying it from genesis
proves the history is internally consistent: every hash links, every merkle root recomputes. It
does not prove that this is the history that existed yesterday, because whoever runs the node
could have rebuilt the whole chain this morning and the replay would still pass.

The standard answer is to publish the head somewhere nobody involved controls. After that,
rewriting history means rewriting a record on a public network, which is not a thing the operator
of this ledger can do.

sections.heading: What is published, and what is not
sections.text:
One memo, six fields, pipe separated:

 

That is the whole payload. No participant, no asset, no amount, no counterparty. A digest and the
position it sits at. The transactions themselves never leave this process, which matters because
a public chain is permanent and personal data on one cannot be withdrawn.

An anchor proves a digest existed at a point in time. It does not prove the contents behind the
digest are true. Nothing can do that from the outside, and claiming otherwise would be the same
mistake the rest of this repository avoids.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.text:
Solana, because the fee is a fraction of a cent, confirmation is seconds, and the memo program
exists for exactly this. There is no SDK underneath it. drunix-gateway/solana.go implements:

- base58, Bitcoin alphabet, for addresses and signatures,
- the compact-u16 (shortvec) length prefix Solana uses in its wire format,
- the legacy message layout: header, account list, recent blockhash, one memo instruction,
- ed25519 signing from the standard library, and the transaction envelope,
- JSON-RPC against the cluster: getSlot , getBalance , getLatestBlockhash , sendTransaction ,
 getSignatureStatuses , getTransaction .

Writing it by hand rather than pulling a dependency has one practical benefit beyond the obvious:
the encodings are unit tested against known vectors with no network and no key, so a wire-format
regression is caught by go test rather than by a cluster silently rejecting a transaction.

sections.heading: Verifying an anchor, as an outsider
sections.text:
Verification reads the transaction off the cluster, pulls the memo out of the logs, finds the block
this ledger holds at that height, and compares the hashes. If they differ it says so: that is the
entire point of the mechanism, so the mismatch path is a reported result and not an error to be
swallowed.

Reads need no account, no key and no funds. Any public RPC endpoint works.

sections.text:
Writing is off in every environment of this project right now: no funded key is configured. The
status endpoint says so in those words rather than implying an anchor exists. Reads and verification

real network without a wallet.

Moving to mainnet is a change of two environment variables and a funded key; the code does not

sections.heading: How the layers divide
sections.text:
The design rule

Every rule about money lives in one place: the settlement core, beside the ledger it protects. The
layers in front of it carry requests and identity and nothing else. If a rule about money can be
found anywhere but the core, that is a bug. 

Concretely: the settlement core is Go, the web app and its API edge are JavaScript, and the edge
forwards settlement calls without deciding anything about them. The edge owns the property register,
KYC and the UPI payment lifecycle; it does not own balances, positions or the chain.

 The five layers
 Layer Responsibility Lives in 
 --- --- --- 
 Experience what each role can see and do, and the public pages anyone may read frontend/src 
 Access establishes who is calling, decides what that caller may touch, and keeps the listing register frontend/api/index.js , server.js 
 Settlement holds the cash leg and the ownership leg, and moves them as one drunix-gateway/umi.go 
 Work escrows a fee against a deliverable, releases it only against anchored evidence drunix-gateway/work .go 
 Record the append-only history every other layer answers to drunix-gateway/chain.go 

The experience and the settlement core deploy independently, so either can be replaced, or fail,
without the other. When the core cannot be reached the app reports unknown ; it never reports a
settlement surface as healthy because it could not ask.

 Authorisation

sections.heading: How the layers divide (continued)
sections.text:
Entitlement is decided in front of the router rather than route by route, so a new surface is covered
the day it ships:

- an unidentified caller is refused with 401, a stranger with 403;
- a supervisor (regulator or admin) may act for someone else where that is the role's job;
- attribution always comes from the authenticated caller, never from a field in the request body;
- reads are scoped as tightly as writes, including diagnostics, receipts and reconciliation views.

Each rule ships with a suite asserting the refused action changed no state.

 The record

Blocks are hash-linked and written to durable storage before in-memory state is updated, so
nothing can be true in the app and missing from the history. A block's transactions are frozen at
commit: contents can never drift from the merkle root they were hashed with, in memory or after a
reload.

If a stored chain fails verification on restore, the rail seals itself and serves read-only rather
than extending history it cannot vouch for. The way back is a supervisor-only repair that records, on
the chain, every height and hash it dropped and who authorised it.

 Two API implementations

sections.heading: How the layers divide (continued)
sections.text:
frontend/api/index.js is the serverless handler production serves. mock-api-server.js is an
Express rig used for local payment testing and as a fixture by several suites. They implement the
same surface and must be patched together . A fix applied to one is live in exactly one
environment.

---

---

 Proof of backing

Tokenised assets fail when issuance outruns the thing behind it. A registrar (or a supervisor)
records a statement for one asset: how many units exist, what they are valued at, the method used,
a hash of the evidence, and how often the statement must be refreshed (90 days by default, one hour
minimum, one year maximum). Issuance is then checked against that figure: anything that would push
the book past the attested units is refused, and the refusal is committed as a block so the gate
itself can be audited.

Four points the layer is careful about:

sections.heading: How the layers divide (continued)
sections.text:
- An asset with no statement behaves exactly as it did before. The gate binds only where someone
 has given it something to bind to.
- Blocking is never reversing. Nothing is burned or unwound; an asset that is already over-issued
 is reported as such rather than quietly corrected.
- A statement that is past its refresh date stops authorising issuance. Stale evidence is evidence
 about the past.
- The attestor cannot be the beneficiary, and the rail says plainly that it checks arithmetic, not
 reality. A false statement here produces a precise, well-evidenced, false number.

Statements are replaced rather than edited, and both the statement and its withdrawal are replayed
from the chain at startup.

 Agent identity

A software actor on the rail acts under a pseudonym rather than under its principal's name. The
principal is split across named custodians with Shamir's secret sharing, and recovering it takes a
threshold of them: a request with a stated trigger, then one approval per custodian, each of which
is a block. Fewer than the threshold recover nothing, which is a property of the arithmetic rather
than a promise.

sections.heading: How the layers divide (continued)
sections.text:
The limits are stated in the API responses, not only here. Every share lives in this one process,
so the protocol is real and the distribution is simulated; real custody means one share per
organisation. The pseudonym is re-identifiable by design, so it remains personal data. A revoked
agent stops acting, but who was accountable for what it already did stays recoverable, and an
identification request that nobody completes lapses and is recorded as an unanswered ask.

Design note, including why the alternative architectures were not chosen:
 AGENT IDENTITY.md .

 Cross-border funding

A buyer outside India cannot be let in by a payment rail alone. A foreign national of non-Indian
origin resident outside India cannot acquire Indian immovable property at all, and for a buyer who
can, the consideration has to arrive in rupees through banking channels: cryptocurrency and digital
tokens are not a permitted method. This layer therefore models the one structure that survives both
facts. A stablecoin is received and converted outside India, and the buyer's rupee wallet is
credited only against a provider attestation carrying a bank advice reference and a purpose code.

sections.heading: How the layers divide (continued)
sections.text:
Eligibility is screened before a quote exists, Travel Rule records are mandatory above the
threshold, the quote carries an expiry, and the destination of the transfer is the off-ramp rather
than the seller. Refusals are committed as blocks for the same reason the other gates commit them.
Nothing is connected to a chain: a transfer reference is recorded, not verified, and the rate is
configured rather than quoted.

Design note, including the research behind it and a separate assessment of token-sale fundraising:
 CROSS BORDER.md .

 Public-chain anchoring

The head of the permissioned ledger is published to a public Solana cluster as a memo carrying the
chain id, block height, block hash and transaction root, and nothing else. Verification reads the
transaction back, finds the local block at that height and compares the hashes, reporting a
mismatch rather than swallowing it.

There is no SDK underneath this: base58, the compact-u16 wire prefix, the legacy message layout and
ed25519 signing are implemented in the module, which means the encodings are unit tested against
known vectors without a network or a key. Reads are live and free; writing needs a funded key and
is off until it has one. Supervisors only, because a fee is spent and publication cannot be undone.

Runbook and the limits of the claim: ANCHORING.md .

 CBDC settlement layer

sections.heading: How the layers divide (continued)
sections.text:
cbdc.go holds the money itself: accounts in integer paise across a retail and a wholesale
segment, issuance and redemption restricted to the central bank role, and KYC tiers that cap
balances and payment sizes on the retail side. Conservation() proves issued equals held plus
redeemed and is served publicly.

Three mechanisms sit on top. Grant and Spend implement purpose-bound money against the
parameters the regulator lists (expiry, merchant category, named merchants, geography), and a
failed condition commits a UMI CBDC REFUSED block rather than returning quietly.
 IssueOffline and RedeemOffline implement the offline path: value is reserved out of the online
balance, the voucher carries an HMAC the accepting device can check without connectivity, and the
nonce index turns a double spend into a deterministic refusal. OpenCondition , SubmitEvent and
 SweepConditions hold money against an attested event, release it to the payee when the named
attestor reports the event, and return it to the payer at the deadline.

Every movement carries a Finality record with the technical and financial parts kept separate,
and an AMLCheck built from the rules and the trained model in the risk layer. Routes live under
 /umi/cbdc/ ; the layer is additive and unmounts cleanly when the rail or chain is absent.

sections.heading: How the layers divide (continued)
sections.text:
Design note, the regulator's published pilot behaviour and the phases still to come:
 CBDC.md .

 Cross-border corridors

 corridors.go carries five rails as separate corridors, each with its own licence requirement,
ceilings, purpose codes and settlement model. Check runs the gate without moving anything;
 Send applies it and then branches on the settlement model.

Atomic corridors move money in a single CBDC transfer and are financially final immediately.
Hash time-locked corridors move it into a per-corridor suspense account, record the hash and the
timeout, and release only against a preimage that is verified rather than trusted; Sweep refunds
an expired lock. Deferred corridors also park the money in suspense and stay provisional until
 ConfirmLeg records the far institution's confirmation. Suspense is an ordinary account on this
ledger, so the CBDC conservation invariant still holds at every step.

Routes live under /umi/corridors/ . Corridor parameters, the precedents they follow and the
limits of the claim: CORRIDORS.md .

 Payment risk: rules and a trained model

 fraud.go is the rule engine: ScorePayment is a pure function over the payment and the payer's
recent history, returning a score, a band, a decision and the weighted factors behind it. It is
hand-written and deterministic, and it is what gates settlement.

sections.heading: How the layers divide (continued)
sections.text:
riskmodel.go is the trained one. A logistic regression over ten features, fitted by
 cmd/trainrisk on a seeded synthetic dataset, with coefficients, feature standardisation and
held-out metrics committed as riskmodel.json and embedded with go:embed . Inference is a dot
product and returns the contributions that produced the score. ExtractRiskFeatures is shared by
the trainer and the server so training and production cannot disagree about what a feature means.

 AssessPayment runs both and reports them side by side with an agreement label
( AGREE CLEAN , AGREE RISKY , RULES ONLY , MODEL ONLY ); the decision field is always the rules'
decision. POST /fraud/assess serves it, GET /fraud/model publishes the card, and the existing
 POST /fraud/score is unchanged.

Model card, generator description and measured numbers: RISK MODEL.md .

sections.heading: The claim this is built to support
sections.text:
The settlement core never knew what a property was.

That is not a slogan, it is a property of the code as written. assetId is an
opaque string everywhere in the rail. There is no assetClass field. DvP moves
 tokens between holders and paise between wallets; the atomic swap has no
opinion about what the tokens represent. pilotISINFor(assetID) is
 sha256("aasthi-pilot-isin " + assetID) , which works on any string.

So adding a second asset class should be a registry entry, not a rewrite. This
document is the plan for proving that, and for being honest about the one place
where carbon genuinely does need new code.

sections.heading: Why carbon, and why not five asset classes
sections.text:
Tokenised real estate settled in central-bank money is the core bet. A second
class is worth adding only if it tests something the first one does not.

Carbon does. Property tokens live forever and change hands. A carbon credit has
a terminal state: it is retired , permanently consumed against someone's
emissions, and must never trade again. That is a lifecycle the rail has never
had to model, and getting it wrong is the single best-known failure mode in
carbon markets: double counting , where the same tonne is claimed twice.

Five shallow asset classes would demonstrate nothing except a dropdown. One
class with a real terminal state and a real conservation invariant is worth
more.

sections.heading: What is additive and what is new
sections.text:
Additive, no behaviour change: 

- assetClass defaults to PROPERTY . An asset with no profile registered is a
 property, exactly as today. Every existing test, seed and settlement path is
 untouched.
- The DvP path, the cash leg, ISIN assignment, reconciliation and the ISO 20022
 trace are not modified. Carbon settles through the same atomic swap.

 Genuinely new: 

- An asset profile registry: class plus the metadata a credit needs (project,
 vintage, methodology, serial range).
- Retirement, which is the only operation property does not have.
- A conservation invariant extended to cover retired supply.

sections.heading: The invariant
sections.text:
Today the securities leg is conserved when:

 outstanding <= authorised

where outstanding is the sum of all positive holder positions.

Retirement removes tokens from circulation without destroying the record of
them. A retired credit is debited from its holder and credited to nobody. So
outstanding falls, and the check above would still pass while quietly losing
track of where the tokens went.

The invariant therefore becomes:

 outstanding + retired <= authorised

This is the part worth looking at closely. It is what makes double counting
detectable rather than merely discouraged: the retired tally is permanent, the
tokens are gone from the book, and the sum cannot exceed what was ever issued.
A credit that was retired cannot be settled again because there is no position
left to move, and cannot be quietly re-issued because authorised is pinned.

sections.heading: Retirement semantics
sections.text:
- Only an asset whose class is CARBON can be retired. Retiring a property is
 refused; it is not a meaningful operation and silently allowing it would make
 the invariant meaningless.
- Retirement is irreversible. There is no un-retire route, by design.
- Each retirement commits a UMI CARBON RETIRED block carrying the holder, the
 quantity, the beneficiary the retirement is claimed for, and the reason.
- The block is the certificate. "Prove this tonne was retired" is answered by a
 block height, not by our word.

sections.heading: Honesty
sections.text:
A real carbon credit is issued and retired in an independent registry, and the
registry is the authority on whether a serial is live or retired. We are not
connected to one. Nothing in this feature talks to an external registry, and
the serial numbers are ours.

So the carbon registry appears on /trust as an eleventh simulated boundary,
in the same words as every other one, and the UI says the same. Specifically we
do not claim conformance with any particular standard's methodology, and we do
not name a registry operator as a partner, because none of them is one.

What is real: the lifecycle, the conservation arithmetic, the irreversibility,
and the block that proves it.

sections.text:
Go, in the rail, as with everything else:
