sections.heading: Governance
sections.text:
Consortium infrastructure succeeds or fails on governance, not cryptography. A permissioned
settlement network validated by a handful of large institutions is not a public blockchain,
whatever the token looks like, and the questions that decide whether it works are the same
ones the card networks and the depositories spent decades on.

This project is a simulation, so it cannot answer those questions for a real network. What
it can do is state them, say what the code currently assumes, and be honest about which
assumptions would not survive contact with a real consortium. Nothing below describes an
agreement with any organisation.

sections.heading: Who may do what, as the code actually stands
sections.text:
Role May do Enforced where 
 --- --- --- 
 Originator create a listing, mint tokens for a validated listing, sell rail authorisation and chaincode endorsement policy 
 Registrar validate a listing, attest a title, withdraw an attestation rail authorisation 
 Investor buy, hold, receive servicing income, delegate bounded authority to an agent rail authorisation 
 Regulator supervisory reads, mint, restate supply, see every blotter rail authorisation 
 Agent only what a mandate grants it, and only for its principal the mandate layer, on the settlement path 

Minting is open to the originator and the regulator as well as the owner. That is a demo
decision, taken so an investor identity holding a listing is not stuck, and it is disclosed
on the trust page rather than buried here. DEMO ROLE SWITCH=false closes the role switcher
that makes the widening reachable.

sections.heading: The five questions
sections.text:
Who is eligible to join, and what is the process. In the code: nobody joins. The
identity set is fixed at five demo participants plus whatever agents a principal delegates
to. There is no onboarding path, no membership committee and no application. A real
deployment needs all three, and the absence is the honest answer rather than an oversight to
be papered over.

 Who sets fees, and can they change. There are no fees anywhere in this system. No
transaction charges a participant, and the settlement asset is simulated wholesale CBDC in
integer paise. Any figure a demo shows is a price between two parties, never a network fee.

 What happens when a validator's commercial interest conflicts with the network's. The
sharpest version here is the attestor: the party that vouches for an asset is usually
connected to the party that benefits from it trading. The code does not resolve the conflict.
What it does is make the attestor's record public, countable and tied to outcomes: who
vouched, how often they withdrew, and who was holding when they did. See
 docs/BACKLOG.md and the attestation layer.

sections.heading: The five questions (continued)
sections.text:
What does exit look like. A participant cannot leave. There is no offboarding,
no settlement of open positions on exit, and no rule about what happens to attestations
signed by a departed attestor. Today a withdrawn attestation leaves its signature valid and
its exposure recorded; a departing attestor would need the same treatment and does not have
it.

 How are smaller participants represented. Not at all. There is one supervisory role and
it can see and do everything. A real consortium has to answer whether the smallest member
has a vote, a veto or only a complaint, and this code takes no position.

sections.heading: What the ledger guarantees, and what it does not
sections.text:
Guaranteed by the code and covered by tests: append-only with detectable tampering, atomic
delivery versus payment in a single block, idempotent settlement, supply conservation,
authority bounded and counted for delegated agents, and signed attestations whose anchor can
be checked independently of this service.

Not guaranteed, and not claimed: legal finality, enforceable accountability for an attestor,
any connection to RBI, SEBI, a depository or a bank, or recovery for a holder who relied on
an attestation that turned out to be wrong. The last one is a governance problem, not a
ledger problem, and it is the one worth arguing about.

sections.heading: Cross-ledger transfer
sections.text:
A tokenised asset that can only exist on one permissioned ledger is a
database row with extra steps. The interesting question is what happens when
a holder wants their position represented somewhere else: a public chain
where they can prove ownership to someone who has never heard of this rail,
or another institution's ledger entirely.

Most answers to that question either hand-wave or quietly create the asset
twice. This one follows the Hyperledger Cacti shape.

sections.heading: The shape
sections.text:
Cacti splits the problem in two, and the code keeps the split visible.

 Connectors , one per ledger, each knowing how to talk to its own chain and
nothing else. There are two: the Drunix fork (this process) and an EVM chain
over JSON-RPC. A connector reports whether it is actually configured, so an
unconfigured one cannot be mistaken for a live integration.

 A business logic plugin , InteropGateway , which sequences a transfer
across connectors and owns the failure handling.

sections.heading: The sequence
sections.text:
Lock and claim, which is the standard asset transfer shape (SATP formalises
it) and the only one where a crash cannot leave the asset in both places.

- LOCK moves the tokens into the interop-custody account in the
 securities ledger. They leave the holder's position, so they cannot be
 settled here while they are represented elsewhere. This is a real ledger
 movement with a block behind it, not a status flag, which means "how much
 of this asset is immobilised" is answered by reading a position.
- COMMIT records the counterpart leg. The tokens stay in custody: that
 custody balance is the amount represented on the other ledger, which is
 what stops the same square metre existing twice.
- ABORT returns the tokens. The holder or a supervisor may do it before
 expiry; after expiry anyone may, because a lock only its beneficiary can
 release is a way to strand someone's asset.

A transfer closes exactly once. Aborting a committed transfer is refused,
which is the bug that has drained real bridges: the holder gets their tokens
back while the remote chain still represents them.

sections.heading: Verified against attested
sections.text:
This is the part worth reading carefully.

With EVM RPC URL and EVM REGISTRY ADDRESS set, a commit carrying a digest
is checked against the remote chain by the connector. If the chain has no
record of it, the commit is refused . If it does, the transfer is marked
 remoteLegVerified: true .

With no connector configured, which is the current state, a commit records a
reference attested by a supervisor. The record says so in words, the flag
stays false, and the statistics count committedVerified and
 committedAttestedOnly separately. Adding them together would be the
dishonest number, so the code never does.

sections.heading: What is real and what is not
sections.text:
Real: the lock, the custody movement, the abort, the expiry rule, the state
machine, the refusals, and the blocks behind every step. These all run on
this rail and the tests cover them, including an attempt to settle a locked
position, which fails.

Not real: anything on a public chain. Nothing here has been bridged to
Sepolia or anywhere else. Pointing the EVM connector at a testnet is a
configuration change rather than new code, but until that is done, a
committed transfer is a claim about another ledger, recorded under the name
of the person who claimed it.

sections.heading: Signing keys, and what happens when one goes bad
sections.text:
On 17 October 2026 a researcher reported that the private keys of eight
eMudhra intermediate certificate authorities could be recovered from their
own public certificates. The keys had not been stolen. They had been
generated with too little randomness, and the private values turned out to
be small integers: 4, 56, 66, 115, 155, 156, 230 and 237. Anyone could
compute them in under a second and then issue a certificate for any website
that browsers would accept. They had been published since April 2025.

Three separate failures stack up in that story, and only the first is about
randomness:

1. a key of catastrophically low quality entered service,
2. nothing checked it again for about eighteen months,
3. withdrawing it meant persuading every browser vendor on earth to ship a
 block list, and a root removal that breaks legitimate sites along the way.

sections.heading: Could it happen here
sections.text:
Honestly: parts of it could, and one part already describes us.

This rail signs credentials, agent passports and attestations with Ed25519.
Before the key register existed, there was no screening of a key before use,
nothing that re-examined it later, and no way to revoke a key at all. A
compromised issuer key would have meant revoking every credential it had
ever signed, one at a time, assuming anybody noticed.

The demo issuer key is derived from a seed published in this repository.
That is the eMudhra situation exactly, with one difference that matters: it
is declared. GET /umi/keys/posture says so, credential verification
reports it, and the summary states that such a credential proves integrity
and not authority. A public key presented as if it were secret is the
dangerous case; a public key labelled public is a demo.

sections.heading: What the register does
sections.text:
GET /umi/keys , and the routes beneath it.

 Screens a key before it enters service. The screen derives the public
keys of every private value a broken generator is likely to emit and refuses
a match: small integers in both byte orders up to 8,192, single repeated
bytes, low-order points, short guessable seeds, and structural degeneracy.
All eight eMudhra values are caught, and they are the fixture the test suite
uses.

 Will not claim more than it can prove. There is no general test for "was
this generated with enough entropy". A key derived from a passphrase nobody
has guessed yet is indistinguishable from a strong one. Every screening
verdict carries that limitation in writing.

 Requires proof of possession. Registering a public key means signing a
server-issued nonce with the private half. Without it, anyone could copy a
public key out of the register and claim it.

 Refuses a key already registered to somebody else. Two holders with one
key is either a copy or a generator repeating itself, and both are the same
failure wearing a different hat.

 Writes everything to the chain, including refusals and audit runs. A
register that records only its successes cannot be audited. This is the
Certificate Transparency idea, and transparency is the only reason an
outsider could check eMudhra at all.

sections.heading: What the register does (continued)
sections.text:
Revokes in one act, effective on the next verification: no block list to
ship, no vendor to wait for. The reason is part of the act, because the
reason decides what happens to past signatures:
 Reason Effect on signatures already made 
 --- --- 
 KEY COMPROMISE Void. If the private key could be computed, nothing it signed proves who signed it. Credentials must be reissued under a new key. 
 SUPERSEDED Stand. An orderly rotation is not an incident. 
 RETIRED Stand. Withdrawn without suspicion. 

 Re-screens keys already in service, on demand, with the result written to
the chain whether it finds anything or not. This is the part that addresses
the eighteen months: a weakness class added to the screen tomorrow is applied
to keys registered today by running one audit, rather than by waiting for an
outsider to report it.

sections.heading: What is still missing
sections.text:
- The screen runs at registration and on audit, not on every verification.
 A scheduled audit is not wired; it is a call somebody has to make.
- Key rotation is modelled as revoke plus register. There is no single
 rotate operation that carries the link between the old key and the new one.
- Hardware-backed keys are not supported. eMudhra's keys were generated on
 certified hardware modules and were still weak, so this would raise the
 floor rather than settle the question.
- The rail's own issuer key is not in the register yet: it is reported by
 GET /umi/keys/posture but registering it would need the key ceremony that
 a production deployment has and a demo does not.

sections.heading: Where to look
sections.text:
- drunix-gateway/keyregistry.go : the screen, the register, revocation, audit.
- drunix-gateway/keyregistry test.go : the eight real eMudhra values as a fixture.
- tests/keyregistry.test.mjs : the same story end to end over HTTP.
- GET /umi/keys , GET /umi/keys/posture .

sections.heading: What was wrong before
sections.text:
A wallet's KYC tier was a string in the request that opened it. The holder was MIN KYC or
 FULL KYC because the caller said so, which made every ceiling built on top of that tier
decoration: the ₹10,000 holding cap and the ₹2,00,000 full-tier cap were enforced faithfully
against a fact nobody had checked.

A tier is now the output of a verification that has a route, evidence, an expiry and an audit
trail. It can no longer be asserted.

sections.heading: What the rules say
sections.text:
The Reserve Bank repealed the consolidated 2016 Master Direction on 28 November 2025 and replaced
it with Directions for each type of regulated entity. The shape implemented here follows the
published position at that replacement.

 Five routes , four of which are also the permitted ways to establish identity inside a video
session: OTP-based Aadhaar e-KYC, offline verification of Aadhaar, a record fetched from the
Central KYC Records Registry against the holder's KYC Identifier, an equivalent e-document of an
officially valid document (including one from DigiLocker), and the video process itself.

 Only the video process is treated as equal to meeting somebody. A customer identified that way
carries no annual debit ceiling and no enhanced due diligence purely for being remote. It has
conditions, and this implementation enforces them rather than assuming them: an identified official
conducting the session, a liveness check, the PAN shown on the call, and the holder's live location
inside India. Miss one and the verification is refused with the list of what was missing.

 OTP-based Aadhaar e-KYC alone is non-face-to-face , so it carries a ₹1,00,000 cumulative annual
debit ceiling and enhanced due diligence until it is converted, typically through a video session.

sections.heading: What the rules say (continued)
sections.text:
An offline Aadhaar file goes stale in three working days. Submit one generated earlier and the
verification is refused, naming the age of the file.

 Periodic updation : two years for high risk, eight for medium, ten for low. Every record carries
its own expiry and reports itself as lapsed once it passes.

 The registry upload window is ten days , with the KYC Identifier handed back to the holder so the
next institution can fetch the record instead of asking for everything again.

sections.heading: The rule that changed the data model
sections.text:
The Aadhaar number must not be stored. Section 8A(4) of the Aadhaar Act bars an offline
verification entity from collecting it at all; an authentication user agency that does receive one
must keep it in a separate encrypted vault, reference it elsewhere by a key, and display at most the
last four digits.

This project is not a licensed user agency and operates no vault. So the honest implementation is
not "store it carefully", it is to refuse it:

 Submit a twelve-digit number in any field and the request is rejected with
 ERR UMI KYC AADHAAR NOT ACCEPTED , explaining that this system does not accept, store or
 transmit Aadhaar numbers.

Refusing is better than silently dropping, which would hide the rule instead of enforcing it. What
is accepted instead is what the offline route actually produces: a reference identifier carrying
the last four digits and a timestamp, with no Aadhaar number behind it. A test asserts that no
block written by this layer contains a twelve-digit number at all.

The same restraint applies to everything else: evidence is kept as a SHA-256 hash, a PAN is kept as
its last four characters after its format is checked, and no document image or video exists.

sections.heading: What is simulated, and said so everywhere
sections.text:
There is no UIDAI authentication call, no upload to the registry, no live video session, no face
match and no liveness check. Those need licences and counterparties this project does not have.
Every response carries that sentence.

What is real: the routes and what each one permits, the refusals and the rule behind each one, the
ceilings that follow from the route rather than from a request field, the expiry, and the fact that
the wallet tier is now written by the verification.

sections.heading: What this is not
sections.text:
No customer risk scoring beyond the band the caller states, no sanctions screening (that is
 docs/AML.md , and the two would be wired together in a real institution), no re-KYC reminders, no
registry reconciliation, no document forgery detection, and no handling of the cases that make real
onboarding hard: minors, non-residents, companies with beneficial owners, and holders who decline
Aadhaar entirely and are entitled to be onboarded anyway.

sections.heading: Performance
sections.text:
Every number on this page was measured on this repository with the command
printed next to it. Nothing here is projected, extrapolated or rounded in the
project's favour, and a result that went the wrong way is reported as such.

Measurements come from a shared cloud machine (2 vCPU). Absolute figures will
differ on other hardware; the comparisons between two versions of the same
code were taken in the same session on the same machine, which is the part
that carries meaning.

sections.heading: Read paths
sections.text:
Bounded page reads. A request for the latest 50 settlements used to
allocate room for the entire book before filling it, so the cost of one page
grew with the age of the deployment. Sizing the copy by the page instead:
 Book size Page Time Allocated 
 --- --- --- --- 
 100 instructions 50 13.7 us 18 KB 
 2,000 instructions 50 7.7 us 18 KB 

The allocation is now the same for both, which is the point: a page costs
what a page costs.

 Asking about one asset. The attestation view asks what settled against a
single asset. It used to take the whole instruction book, including every
ISO 20022 message trace, and discard almost all of it. With 40 assets and
2,000 settlements on the rail, filtering inside the rail instead:
 Approach Time Allocated 
 --- --- --- 
 Filter under the rail's lock 88 us 18 KB 
 Copy everything, then filter 797 us 705 KB 

That is about nine times faster and thirty-eight times less memory per call.

 Where it does not help. When nearly every row matches, for example a rail
carrying one asset and 2,000 trades against it, the filtered path is slightly
slower than copying the book, because it walks the index twice to size the
result exactly: 882 us against 643 us, with the same allocation. The
realistic shape for this call is many assets and a question about one, so the
trade is worth taking, but it is a trade and not a free win.

sections.heading: Bounds on every list route
sections.text:
A list endpoint without a ceiling is a way to make the server allocate. Every
route that reads ?limit= now goes through one helper with a default and a
maximum, and a test pins the behaviour, including that a nonsense value falls
back to the default rather than to everything.
 Route Default Ceiling 
 --- --- --- 
 settlement instructions 50 500 
 servicing history 100 500 
 ledger blocks 50 500 
 credentials 50 200 
 mandates 50 200 
 interop transfers 50 200 
 notifications 50 200

sections.heading: Front end
sections.text:
The settlement page loads five panels that sit below the forms people
actually came for. Splitting them out of the page chunk:
 Chunk Before After 
 --- --- --- 
 settlement page 69.4 KB 35.9 KB 

The panels now arrive as five separate chunks between 3 KB and 11 KB, fetched
when the page renders them. Total bytes for someone who scrolls the whole
page are slightly higher; bytes before first paint are roughly halved.

sections.heading: Settlement throughput
sections.text:
The throughput figure shown in the application is measured by a Go benchmark
and labelled as a benchmark rather than as a live rate, because it is one.
The application states both the measured figure and the much lower ceiling
observed through the full HTTP path, and marks the live number as not
measured. That labelling is deliberate and should not be quietly improved.

sections.heading: What has not been optimised
sections.text:
- The serverless API handler is one large file. It is a cold-start cost and a
 maintenance cost, and splitting it is not yet done.
- The rail keeps its working set in memory and replays it from the ledger on
 boot. There is no eviction, so a very long-lived deployment grows. For the
 demo's lifetime this is fine; for a real one it is not.
- No load test exists. Throughput under concurrency is unmeasured, and this
 page does not claim a figure for it.

sections.heading: Private data collections
sections.text:
Settlement needs two things that pull in opposite directions. Everyone on the
network has to agree on what happened, and some of what happened is nobody
else's business. A participant's identity evidence and the price a bilateral
trade was struck at are both facts the ledger has to be able to prove, and
neither is a fact the rest of the network is entitled to read.

Hyperledger Fabric answers this with private data collections, and that is the
pattern implemented here.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.text:
A collection is a named side database with a membership policy. Members hold
the value. Every peer, member or not, holds the hash of the key and the hash
of the value on the public ledger. So the network can prove a record exists,
prove it has not changed since it was committed, and order it against every
other transaction, while the contents stay with the organisations entitled to
them.

On this rail:

sections.heading: How it works (continued)
sections.text:
- Collection definitions are public, served at GET /umi/private/collections .
 Fabric puts the collection config on the public ledger for the same reason:
 a policy nobody can read is not a policy anyone can check.
- A write commits a UMI PDC WRITE block carrying the collection name, the
 key hash, the value hash and the member roles. Nothing derived from the
 value except its hash. The key is hashed too, because here the key is a
 participant id, which is personal data in its own right.
- A read by a member returns the value. A read by anyone else returns 403 
 and the proof . That is the mechanism working, not a leak: refusing the
 value while publishing the hash is the entire point.
- Anyone can verify a value they already hold:
 POST /umi/private/{collection}/{key}/verify . The hash is the SHA-256 of
 the value serialised as JSON with sorted keys, so a counterparty can compute
 it themselves without this code.
- blockToLive purges the value and keeps the proof, which is how an
 append-only ledger lives with a retention limit.

sections.heading: The collections
sections.text:
Collection Members Also readable by Retention 
 --- --- --- --- 
 kycEvidence registrar, regulator, admin the subject of the record kept 
 settlementTerms regulator, admin the named counterparties purged after 500 blocks 

Writing is always a member act. Being the person a KYC record is about does
not make you the registrar who attests it, so a subject can read their own
record and cannot write it.

sections.heading: What this generalises
sections.text:
The rail already had one instance of this idea: KYC evidence anchored by
digest only in the document register, where the bytes are never stored and no
code path can serve them. That works, but it is a single hard-coded case
expressed as scattered checks on a document type. A collection states the same
rule as data, applies it to anything, and makes the policy inspectable over
HTTP.

sections.heading: What is real and what is not
sections.text:
Real: the policy, the hashes on the chain, the refusal path, independent
verification, the blockToLive purge and the ledger evidence for both the
write and the purge.

Not real: the distribution. Fabric gossips private data only between
authorised peers, so a value never reaches a non-member's disk at all. This
rail is a single process, so membership is enforced in code rather than by the
value never arriving. Nothing here should be read as a claim that an operator
with the process memory cannot see a value. Running the rail as real Fabric
peers, one per organisation, with these collections declared in the chaincode
collection config, is what would close that gap.

sections.heading: Restart behaviour
sections.text:
A restart replays the UMI PDC WRITE blocks, so the proofs come back and
verification keeps working. The values do not come back, because they were
never on the chain. A recovered record reports valueAvailable: false with a
note saying why, rather than looking like an empty record. That is the
mechanism being honest about itself: if a restart could restore the values
from the chain, the values would have been on the chain.

sections.heading: Why it exists separately from the rules
sections.text:
The rail has screened UPI Collect payments since the first week, with
hand-written rules: amount bands, velocity counts, a structuring window, a
small list of suspicious VPA fragments. Those rules are useful, fast and fully
explainable, and they are not machine learning. For a while the code described
them as an "ML-pluggable" interface, which is the sort of phrasing that lets a
reader hear "AI" without anything having been trained. That wording is gone.

What replaces it is an actual trained classifier, fitted in this repository,
with its coefficients committed to source control and its measurements
published next to them. The rules still decide. The model is a second opinion
that has to show its working.

sections.heading: What it is
sections.text:
A logistic regression over ten features, fitted by batch gradient descent with
L2 regularisation. Ten coefficients, one bias, one mean and one standard
deviation per feature. Inference is a dot product: microseconds, no service
call, no key, nothing to be unavailable.

Linear and small is a choice, not a limitation we are apologising for. A
gradient-boosted tree would score a little better and would not be able to tell
a payer in one sentence why their payment was flagged. Every score this model
produces comes back with the features that moved it and by how much.

sections.heading: What it was trained on
sections.text:
Synthetic data. 12,000 generated payments, 70/30 split. 

Nobody has given this project labelled payment fraud. Real labels come from
banks and they do not leave banks. So the training set is generated by a seeded
program in the repository rather than collected, and every surface that reports
a metric says so: the model card endpoint, the weights file, the code comments
and this page.

The generator builds two overlapping populations:

- Ordinary payments: amounts clustered around a personal norm, one or two
 payments in a day, verified identity, daytime, an account that has existed
 for a while.
- Fraudulent shapes drawn from what investigators describe: amounts parked just
 under a reporting threshold, repeated near-identical amounts, bursts of
 payments within minutes, large sums from accounts minutes old, activity
 between midnight and five in the morning.

Two deliberate contaminations keep the problem honest. Roughly a fifth of the
fraudulent payments are careful enough to look ordinary, and a tenth of the
ordinary ones carry a shape that looks wrong (a property purchase against a
quiet history, a new account buying in). Two percent of labels are flipped,
because real fraud labels are decided by tired people reading incomplete files.

sections.heading: What it was trained on (continued)
sections.text:
Without that contamination the model scored a held-out AUC of 1.000, which does
not mean it was good. It means the generator was separating the classes on the
model's behalf. A clean 1.000 in a report like this should always be read as a
defect in the evaluation.

sections.heading: Features
sections.text:
Feature Meaning 
 --- --- 
 log amount log of the payment amount in rupees 
 amount vs recent mean this amount over the payer's recent average, capped at 10 
 txn count 10m payments by this payer in the last ten minutes 
 txn count 24h payments by this payer in the last day 
 log total 24h log of the payer's rupee total over the last day 
 log account age min log of the account age in minutes 
 kyc verified 1 when KYC is complete 
 near threshold how far under a 50k / 2L / 10L reporting line the amount sits, 0 to 1 
 repeat amount share share of recent payments within five percent of this amount 
 odd hour 1 when the payment lands between midnight and five, Indian time 

Training and inference call the same extraction function. A feature computed
one way during training and another way in production is the most common way a
model quietly stops working, so there is only one implementation of it and a
test asserts the weights file and the extractor agree on the order.

sections.heading: Measured results
sections.text:
Held out, on rows the fit never saw, with the operating threshold chosen on the
training split only:
 Metric Value 
 --- --- 
 AUC 0.824 
 Accuracy 0.860 
 Precision 0.626 
 Recall 0.719 
 F1 0.670 
 Held-out rows 3,600 
 Base rate about 18 percent 

Read that honestly. Catching roughly seven in ten of the generated fraud at
about six in ten precision is a useful second opinion and nothing like a
finished anti-fraud system. It is also a number about the generator, not about
Indian payments.

The live figures are served from the weights file rather than copied by hand,
so this table cannot drift away from the model without a test noticing.

sections.heading: What it is not allowed to do
sections.text:
- It does not decide. The published rules make the call. The combined
 assessment returns both scores and labels the agreement between them, which is
 the case a reviewer most needs to see: the payments where the two differ.
- It does not block anybody's money. A model trained on invented data
 stopping a real settlement would be indefensible.
- It does not see anything beyond the payment and the payer's recent
 history. No identity attributes, no geography, no device, no counterparty
 profile.

sections.heading: Retraining
sections.text:
The seed is fixed, so a rerun on the same code produces the same file. Changing
the generator, the features or the hyperparameters changes the weights and the
published metrics together: the numbers on this page come from the same run
that produced the coefficients, and there is no path by which one can be
updated without the other.

sections.heading: What to build next
sections.text:
Written 19 October 2026, against 774261e plus the proof-page fixes.

This is a working plan, not a wish list. Everything here is sized, ordered and justified by
something the codebase actually lacks. Items already shipped live in docs/BACKLOG.md under the
closed table; deferred audit findings stay there too. If an item below turns out to be wrong when
it is picked up, the right move is to say so and drop it, not to build it anyway.

sections.heading: The one sentence version
sections.text:
The settlement core is strong and the story above it is now complete (asset, attestor, credential,
token, and conditional payment on a verified result). The two real weaknesses are operational
credibility (one untested module, no linting, hand-maintained duplicate APIs) and the first
ninety seconds of a stranger's visit (no screenshots, no hosted walkthrough, demo data with junk
in it). Those should be fixed before any new feature.

---

sections.heading: P0 · Correctness and credibility
sections.text:
1. Close the conditional settlement loop on the cash leg
The work desk now pays on a verified result. The DvP cash leg still cannot: it settles atomically
or fails, with nothing in between. The missing shape is cash locked at settlement and released
when a named condition is met, where the condition is the presentation of a valid credential and
the party allowed to assert it may be an agent under a mandate. This is the piece that makes the
three layers (credential, mandate, escrow) one mechanism rather than three demos.

Done looks like: a UMI CONDITION block family, the reconciliation check proving conservation
while cash sits conditional, a timeout that cannot strand money, and a failure test for every way
the condition can fail to arrive.

 2. Test the untested module
 api-gateway has no tests at all ( docs/BACKLOG.md D1). It is the only Go module in that state.
Either cover it or delete it: an untested module in a repository that advertises its test counts
is worse than no module.

 3. One API implementation, not two
 frontend/api/index.js and mock-api-server.js are maintained by hand in parallel (D5). They
have already drifted once. Extract the shared handlers so the test rig and production cannot
diverge silently.

sections.heading: P0 · Correctness and credibility (continued)
sections.text:
4. Lint
No ESLint config exists (D2). The result is inconsistent style and a class of bug (unused state,
missing dependency arrays, shadowed variables) that nothing currently catches. Add a config and
wire it into CI as a non-blocking job first, then make it blocking once the backlog is clear.

---

sections.heading: P1 · Reproducibility
sections.text:
5. A compose file for the whole app
Three processes have to be started in the right order by hand (D4). One compose file, one command,
documented ports. This is the single biggest reduction in "I cloned it and nothing happened".

 6. A seed that is not embarrassing
Three probe listings and two broken pincodes are still in the demo data (D6), the attestor record
reads "100% withdrawn (8 of 8)" because the test suite withdraws everything it issues, and demo
wallets accumulate state across runs. A deterministic, curated seed with a reset command would fix
all three. Nobody should see a 100% withdrawal rate on the page that argues attestors matter.

 7. Rotate the two credentials still listed as unrotated
D7. A demo key in a public repository is a small risk and a large credibility cost.

---

sections.heading: P2 · First impression
sections.text:
8. Screenshots and a recorded walkthrough
The README describes screens nobody can see without running the stack. Real screenshots of the
ledger explorer, the settlement rail and the proof chain, plus a two-minute recording of the demo
script, would do more for a visitor than any new feature on this list.

 9. A hosted read-only instance that stays seeded
The public deployment loses its interesting state. A nightly reseed, or a read-only snapshot
instance, means the links in the README show something instead of an empty rail.

 10. Interface consistency, done carefully
The signed-in screens are visibly older than the landing page. The first attempt at this (a
component library across three pages at once) was reverted because it changed too much at once.
The right version is: one page, behind a flag, reviewed on the running site, then the next. Start
with the ledger explorer, which is the page a sceptic opens first.

---

sections.heading: P3 · Depth, once the above is done
sections.text:
11. A second interop route
One hash-locked transfer pattern is thin cover against the fragmentation criticism. A
notary-attested route alongside it would show the asset model is transport independent.

 12. Attestor accountability with teeth
The record publishes an attestor's history and states plainly that no penalty is enforced. The
honest next step is a staking or bonding model where a withdrawal has a cost, or a clear written
argument for why that belongs to the legal layer and not the rail.

 13. Make the agent path demonstrable end to end
An agent can now hold a mandate, deliver work under it and be paid on verification. Nothing in the
repository drives that sequence automatically. A scripted agent (clearly labelled as a script, not
an autonomous system) that runs the whole loop would make the most topical part of the project
visible in thirty seconds.

 14. Pagination in the interface, not just the API
List reads are bounded server side. The pages still render everything they receive. For a demo
dataset that is fine; it would not survive a real one.

---

sections.heading: Deliberately not doing
sections.text:
- More asset classes. Five shallow ones would add surface and no credibility.
- A token, a chain or a listing of any kind. The project's argument is that settlement is the
 interesting part.
- Claiming any real integration. The rail is a simulation of the UMI pattern, the Fabric fork
 is a fork, the talent provider is a pattern not a vendor. That stays true in every surface.

sections.heading: Taking the EVM connector live on Sepolia
sections.text:
The cross-ledger gateway ( docs/INTEROP.md ) ships with its EVM connector
unconfigured, and says so everywhere it is shown. This is the runbook that
moves that boundary from simulated to live. It is configuration plus a
contract deployment: no code changes, which is the point of putting the
connector behind an interface in the first place.

Nothing in this document has been run against Sepolia. It is written from the
code that would do it, and the fact that it is untried is exactly why the
trust page still says the connector is not configured.

sections.heading: What you need, and what you do not
sections.text:
Read and write have very different requirements here, and the first version
of this document ran them together. They are separate:

 To verify cross-ledger commits (the interop connector), you need only an RPC
URL. The check is eth call against verifyDigest , which is a read. No
account, no private key, no Sepolia ETH. Any public Sepolia endpoint works.

 To write document anchors (the mirror in evm mirror.go ), you need more,
and the current code cannot do it through a hosted provider. It calls
 eth sendTransaction , which asks the node to sign. Infura, Alchemy and the
endpoint behind MetaMask hold no keys for you, so they reject it. Writing
needs either a node that holds an unlocked account (anvil, geth, a local
signer in front of the provider) or local signing in the mirror, which is not
written yet.

So for the interop work the sequence is: deploy the registry once from a
wallet you already control, then give the rail a read-only RPC URL and the
contract address. Deployment is the only step that spends gas.

sections.heading: 1. Deploy the registry
sections.text:
contracts/DocumentRegistry.sol is the contract the connector talks to. It
stores an anchor per document: the CID key, the SHA-256 digest, the asset id,
a type and a validity window, with a registrar allowlist for writes and
 verifyDigest(bytes32) open to everyone for reads.

 contracts/deploy.js and contracts/deploy-local.mjs are the existing
deployment paths. Deploy to Sepolia, then note the address.

Give the sending account the registrar role:

 

Without it every anchor reverts, while reads keep working, so a missing
registrar role looks like "writes silently fail and verification always says
no".

sections.heading: EVM_SENDER_ADDRESS=0x<account with the registrar role>
sections.text:
Restart. Two things change on their own:

- GET /umi/interop reports the EVM connector as configured: true and the
 status line becomes the RPC URL and contract address.
- A commit carrying a digest is now checked against Sepolia. If the chain has
 no record of it the commit is refused rather than recorded, and the
 transfer stays LOCKED so the holder can still abort and get their tokens
 back.

The same variables also switch on the existing document mirror
( evm mirror.go ). Against a hosted provider its writes will fail, for the
signing reason above, and that failure is contained: anchoring to the local
chain is unaffected and no settlement can fail because of it. KYC evidence is
excluded from the mirror by design and stays excluded.

sections.heading: a digest the chain has never seen must be refused, not recorded
sections.text:
curl -s -X POST https://<rail-host /umi/interop/XCHAIN-000001/commit \
 -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -H 'X-Identity-Role: Regulator' -H 'X-Identity-Id: regulator1' \
 -d '{"remoteTxRef":"0x0","digest":"'"$(printf 'nothing' sha256sum cut -d" " -f1)"'"}'

sections.heading: want: ERR_UMI_INTEROP_STATE, "evm has no record of that digest"
sections.text:
The refusal is the test that matters. A connector that accepts anything is
worse than no connector, because it turns an attestation into something that
reads like a confirmation. Both directions are covered by
 TestConfiguredConnectorVerifiesTheRemoteLeg and
 TestConfiguredConnectorRefusesAnUnbackedCommit , which run against a stub
JSON-RPC node that speaks the same eth call the real contract answers.

sections.heading: 4. Update the trust page
sections.text:
/trust reads EVM RPC URL and EVM REGISTRY ADDRESS for the public chain
mirror row, so that one flips on its own. The cross-ledger row is written as
simulated in prose and has to be edited by hand once a transfer has actually
been verified against Sepolia. Do not edit it before that: the row is about
what has happened, not what is configured.

sections.heading: What this still would not be
sections.text:
A verified commit proves the remote chain holds the digest. It does not mint
anything on Sepolia, and there is no ERC-20 or ERC-721 representing the
asset over there. The locked tokens are immobilised here against evidence
recorded there, which is an anchor, not a bridge. Issuing a real token on the
remote side, and burning it to release the lock, is the next piece of work
and is not written.

sections.heading: Testing
sections.text:
Every number on this page came from running the command next to it on 14 October 2026, on a clean
checkout at commit 4e6da94 . If a figure here disagrees with what you get, the page is stale:
please open an issue rather than assuming your machine is wrong.

sections.heading: What each command actually covers
sections.text:
make test : the integration sweep

Runs regression.sh , which does two things: a direct list of HTTP checks against the app and the
rail, and then every file matching tests/ .test.mjs .
 
 --- --- 
 Command bash regression.sh 
 Needs the app on :8080 and the rail on :21100 ( make dev ) 
 Suite files 104 in tests/ 
 Reported result 149 passed, 0 failed 

One hazard worth knowing before a repeat run: anything already listening on :8080 or :21100 
is the enemy of a trustworthy result. A leftover app answers with a different admin key and a
dozen suites fail for reasons that have nothing to do with the code. make test-fresh now clears
those strays rather than starting a process that cannot bind, and scripts/dev-stack.sh refuses
to report a healthy stack it did not actually start.

 tests/credentials.test.mjs is worth running on its own when touching the rail proxy. It
verifies a credential's Ed25519 signature inside the test process, using only the issuer's
published key, so it fails if anything between the rail and the client alters a single byte
of a signed document.

 

 tests/proofpage.test.mjs guards the proof page: it reads the page source to prove no bare
 fetch has crept back in (one did, and it made the agent authority tab unusable for everybody),
then calls each route the page reads as a signed-in participant.

sections.heading: What each command actually covers (continued)
sections.text:
tests/outcome.test.mjs covers outcome-based settlement on the work desk: criteria that
cannot be edited after the engagement opens, a verifier who is neither party, verification
that does not move money by itself, a dispute window that only the clock or the funder can
shorten, and a failed check that freezes the escrow instead of paying it out. It uses a one
second window so the timing path is actually exercised rather than asserted.

 tests/mandates.test.mjs covers delegated authority: an agent settling on a principal's
behalf. It drives the Go rail directly rather than the web proxy, because the proxy only
recognises the five named demo identities and files anything else as investor1 , which
would hide the very thing under test. The rail is where every bound is enforced.
 Runtime about 50 seconds 

 Read the number carefully. The 143 is the count of top-level checks the sweep reports: each
direct HTTP assertion counts once, and each suite file counts once however many assertions it
contains. Individual suites print their own totals, which are finer grained. For example
 verifyproperty reports 29 assertions and pincodecheck reports 26, but each contributes 1 to the
143. There is no single meaningful "total assertions" figure, and this project does not publish
one.

sections.heading: What each command actually covers (continued)
sections.text:
Three suites are skipped by the api CI job and run in the contracts job instead, because they
need solc , a local EVM chain and the reference IPFS hasher: contracts , cidconformance ,
 evmmirror . Locally they run if you have the toolchain and are reported as failures if you do not,
which is deliberate. A test that silently skips is worse than one that fails loudly.

 make test-go : the Go modules

Runs scripts/go-tests.sh : gofmt -l , go vet and go test -race -count=1 for each module in
turn. There is no single module graph in this repository, so a root-level go test ./... cannot
work.

 api-gateway 0 0 no test files 

 api-gateway having no tests is a real gap, not an oversight in this document. It is listed as a
good first issue in CONTRIBUTING.md .

 make smoke : the frontend renders

Builds the bundle with vite.smoke.config.js and renders every route in Node, failing if any route
produces an error boundary instead of content. This exists because a route can compile perfectly
and still throw on first paint.

 Command cd frontend && npm run smoke 
 Needs nothing running 
 Catches render-time crashes, missing providers, bad imports 
 Does not catch anything that needs a backend, and anything visual

sections.heading: What each command actually covers (continued)
sections.text:
make secret-scan : tracked credentials

 scripts/secret-scan.sh greps every tracked file for things shaped like live credentials: GitHub
tokens, PayU salts and merchant keys, inline admin keys. Known placeholders ( devkey , testsalt ,
 example ) are allowed. It runs inside the regression sweep as well, so a secret cannot pass

 npm run build : the lint proxy

 There is no ESLint configuration in this repository. ESLint 10 refuses to run without one, so
the frontend has no lint gate today. Until one exists, npm run build and node --check are what
catch syntax and import errors. Adding a flat config is a good first issue.

---

sections.heading: How much of the rail do these checks actually touch?
sections.text:
A pass count is not a coverage figure. Ninety-eight suites passing says nothing about how much of
the rail they reach, and the honest way to find out is to measure it rather than assume.

The approach is borrowed from Scapia's write-up of their Argus test lab (October 2026). Their
second tool is the interesting one: map every action a user can take, replay the suite against that
map on paper, and give each action one of three verdicts. Their own published answer was
uncomfortable (24.6% of commerce actions certainly covered, one vertical under 2%) and publishing
it was the point.

 node scripts/coverage-rail.mjs the figure, by area
 node scripts/coverage-rail.mjs --gaps exactly what nothing reaches

The tool reads source only, starts nothing and executes nothing, so the same commit gives the same
number on any machine. It builds the catalogue from the route table declared at the top of each
server file, cross-checks every declared path against the registered routes so the catalogue cannot
drift into fiction, then replays each suite's requests against it.
 Verdict Meaning 
 --- --- 
 covered a suite certainly issues this method against this path 
 possible a suite reaches the path, but the method is not provable from the source 
 not covered nothing in the suite reaches it

sections.heading: How much of the rail do these checks actually touch? (continued)
sections.text:
As measured: 64% of 100 rail actions are certainly covered, 16% are possible, and the rest
are reached by nothing. tests/coverage.test.mjs recomputes this on every run and fails if the
published figure drifts from the measured one, if coverage falls below its floor, or if a declared
route stops being served.

The measurement earned its keep immediately. It showed that POST /umi/cbdc/transfer and
 POST /umi/cbdc/redeem were exercised by nothing at all: the conservation identity was being
asserted without either of the two paths that can break it. The Travel Rule refusal and the
corridor dry run were in the same state. Those now have tests, which is how the figure moved from
51.2% to 58.1%, and the interoperability layer arrived with its own suite.

sections.heading: Does the suite catch anything? Planted defects
sections.text:
A green suite has two possible meanings and no way to tell them apart: the code is correct, or the
assertions are weak. Argus had the same problem, and settled it by deleting a real feature on a
branch to see whether the suite noticed.

 node scripts/plant-defect.mjs plant each defect, run the suite that should notice
 node scripts/plant-defect.mjs aml-threshold

Each defect is a mistake somebody could plausibly make in review: a threshold nudged out of reach, a
guard dropped, a refusal softened. The harness edits the file, rebuilds and restarts the rail, runs
the one suite that should fail, then restores the file in a finally block. It refuses to start if
the files it touches have uncommitted changes.
 Planted defect Caught 
 --- --- 
 Screening stops blocking (block threshold raised out of reach) yes, 5 checks 
 The Aadhaar refusal is removed, so a twelve digit number is accepted yes, 2 checks 
 A video session without liveness is treated as face-to-face yes, 2 checks 
 The Travel Rule check passes with the parties unnamed yes, 3 checks 
 The proposing agent stops re-reading its evidence before acting no, first time; yes, 3 checks, now 

All five are caught as of the current commit. One was not, and that is the row worth reading.

sections.heading: Does the suite catch anything? Planted defects (continued)
sections.text:
The last row is why the harness exists. Removing the agent's freshness check broke nothing any test
could see, because the suite accepted either outcome at that point and only the Go unit test
covered staleness. Worse, the hole was real in the code as well: the freshness check handled AML
cases but never conditional payments, so a proposal about a payment that had already been released
would have been approved and acted on. Both are fixed, and the scenario is now tested end to end.

These are five planted defects, not a proof. They say the suite notices these five specific
mistakes, and nothing about the ones nobody thought of.

sections.heading: Continuous integration
sections.text:
.github/workflows/ci.yml runs on pushes and pull requests to main , with permissions:
contents: read and no secrets exposed to any job.

 --- ---

sections.heading: Writing a test here
sections.text:
Suites are plain Node, no framework. The shape is consistent across the directory:

 

Two rules that matter more than style:

1. Sabotage your own test before trusting it. Break the code it covers, confirm it fails, and
 confirm it fails for the right reason. A sabotage that does not compile proves nothing. Several
 assertions in this repository were found to be vacuous exactly this way.
2. Cold-start the stack before believing a single failure. The sweep is not idempotent across
 runs on one long-lived stack, and make test-fresh is that restart in one command. The usual
 cause is the fraud engine rather than drift: the velocity rule counts the demo payer's payments
 over ten minutes, every run uses the same demo identity, so a second run inside that window is
 blocked on purpose and three suites fail with FAILED FRAUD BLOCKED . The sweep now says so when
 it sees that status, instead of leaving the reader to conclude the repository is broken.

---

sections.heading: Known limitations
sections.text:
- No end-to-end browser test. The render smoke proves routes mount; it does not click through a
 purchase. The closest thing to a full journey check is the integration sweep plus the manual
 walkthrough in DEMO.md .
- No coverage measurement is published. None is collected, so no percentage is claimed.
- No load or soak testing. The throughput figures in THROUGHPUT.md come from
 Go benchmarks on one machine and are labelled measured:false where they are derived rather than
 observed.
- The Fabric network under network/ is not exercised by CI. It needs Docker and the Fabric
 binaries, and nothing in the demo path depends on it.
- api-gateway is untested , as noted above.

sections.heading: The constraint
sections.text:
Every settlement takes one lock. SettleDvP holds r.mu across the whole
critical section: check the cash, check the securities, move both legs, append
the block. Settlements cannot overlap.

That is deliberate. The invariants this rail exists to guarantee are:

- no central bank money is created or destroyed,
- no token is created or destroyed,
- both legs settle or neither does.

A single writer is the simplest arrangement in which those cannot be violated.
Optimistic concurrency, or striping the lock per wallet, would both be faster
and would each open a window in which a reader can observe one leg without the
other. The rail is correct first and fast second, and the figures below are the
ceiling that choice buys.

sections.heading: Measured
sections.text:
Two sources, both real, measuring different things.

 The engine, from the Go benchmark

Run it yourself:

 cd drunix-gateway && go test -bench BenchmarkSettleDvP -run XXX -benchtime 3000x

On the 2 vCPU container used during development:
 Benchmark ns/op Derived p50 p99 
 --- --- --- --- --- 
 BenchmarkSettleDvP 37,911 about 26,000 settlements/sec 0.027 ms 0.131 ms 
 BenchmarkSettleDvPContended 40,418 about 24,700 settlements/sec mean lock wait under 1 us max 2 queued 

The contended run barely differs from the serial one, for an unexciting reason
worth stating rather than hiding: the box has 2 vCPUs, so at most two
goroutines were ever really running. This is not evidence that the lock scales.
It is evidence that we did not have enough parallelism available to prove
anything either way.

 The live endpoint

 GET /umi/throughput reports what this process has actually served. After 25
settlements over HTTP on the same container:

 settlements 25, settled 25, failed 0
 latency ms p50 0.17, p95 0.243, p99 0.252, max 0.297
 lockWait ms mean 0, max 0
 serial ceiling 5,711/sec at that mean latency

Lock wait is zero because the requests arrived one at a time, so nothing ever
queued. That is the honest reading: under this load the lock is not the
constraint, and the figure is bounded by the work itself.

sections.heading: Measured (continued)
sections.text:
Note the two numbers disagree: about 26,000/sec from the benchmark against
about 5,700/sec live. The difference is the rest of the handler, the JSON, and
a container under other load. The lower number is the more useful one, and
neither is a production figure.

sections.heading: The other money paths
sections.text:
The figures above describe DvP settlement and nothing else. A CBDC transfer,
a programmable-money spend and a corridor send do different work, take
different locks and cost different amounts, so quoting the DvP number for
them would be quoting a measurement of something else. That gap was listed as
an open item and this closes it.

 GET /umi/pathspeed reports the same shape per path: calls, completed,
refused, latency percentiles, lock wait, and a line saying what work the path
actually does. Refusals are counted and timed apart from completions, because
a refusal returns before the work it refused and folding the two together
would flatter the average. A path with no traffic is omitted rather than
reported as zero.

The synthetic companion, on the same 2 vCPU container, median of three runs at
 -benchtime 3000x :
 Benchmark ns/op Derived What it does 
 --- --- --- --- 
 BenchmarkCorridorCheck 377 about 2,650,000/sec Licences, caps, Travel Rule and monthly usage. Moves nothing. 
 BenchmarkCBDCIssue 20,866 about 47,900/sec Cap check, balance, supply counter, one block. 
 BenchmarkSettleDvP 33,024 about 30,200/sec Both legs plus the block, under one lock. 
 BenchmarkCBDCTransfer 46,238 about 21,600/sec AML screen, caps, both balances, one block. 

Two things in that table are worth reading rather than skimming.

sections.heading: The other money paths (continued)
sections.text:
A CBDC transfer costs more than a DvP settlement. That looks wrong until you
look at the work: the transfer runs an AML screen, and the screen is the
expensive part, not the money movement. Screening is not optional and the cost
belongs in the figure.

A corridor check is roughly a hundred times cheaper than anything that moves
money, because it deliberately moves nothing. It is the pricing and
eligibility pass. Quoting it as "corridor speed" would be the dishonest
version of this table.

The transfer benchmark rotates payers. The AML velocity rule blocks a payer
after eight payments in ten minutes, which is correct behaviour, and a
benchmark that tripped it would be timing the refusal path while claiming to
time the transfer path.

Run them:

 cd drunix-gateway && go test -run XXX -bench "BenchmarkCBDC BenchmarkCorridor" -benchtime 3000x -count=3

sections.heading: What these numbers are not
sections.text:
- Not end to end. They measure the settlement engine. They exclude the HTTP
 layer, the JSON, the proxy hop through the web app, and the network. A real
 client's experience is dominated by those.
- Not with a database. The measurements above ran with no DATABASE URL .
 With the Postgres mirror attached, every settlement also does a write, and
 that write will dominate. Expect a figure lower by an order of magnitude or
 more.
- Not a competitor to a published chain benchmark. Numbers produced by a
 harness against a configured network, on known hardware, are a different
 measurement from an in-process loop. An in-process loop will always look
 better and always mean less.
- Not a capacity plan. One container, one process, no replication.

sections.heading: What would raise the ceiling
sections.text:
Partitioning by asset.

Every invariant here is per-asset or per-wallet. There is no rule that spans
two unrelated properties, so two settlements touching disjoint assets have no
reason to serialise against each other. A shard per asset, with the cash leg
partitioned by wallet, would let them proceed in parallel without weakening any
guarantee. Cross-asset operations (baskets) would take the shards in a fixed
order to avoid deadlock.

That is a design, not an implementation. It is not built, it is not claimed as
a capability, and the panel in the UI says so.

sections.heading: Work Orders: escrowed property work, settled on completion
sections.text:
Status: design + implementation (this document ships with the code).
 Context: gig-work marketplaces are built on one idea, that a contract links pay to task
completion . This module is where that idea lands inside AasthiChain. No external provider is
integrated or named: the talent boundary is an adapter, and it runs as a simulation.

---

sections.heading: 1. The problem this solves
sections.text:
AasthiChain tokenises a property and settles trades atomically on the Aasthi Settlement
Interface (ASI). What it has never modelled is the cost of keeping the asset real .

A tokenised building still needs inspecting, repairing, revaluing, photographing, and its
title re-verified. Today all of that happens off-ledger, on trust, paid by somebody on an
invoice nobody can audit. For an investor holding 400 tokens of a Pune apartment, the
maintenance spend is the single largest unexplained hole in the model.

That gap has the same shape as the one ASI already closed for trading: two things that
must happen together, work delivered and money paid , with no honest way to make
them simultaneous. ASI's answer was atomic DvP. This module applies the identical
discipline to labour.

sections.heading: 2. The guarantee
sections.text:
The fee leaves the funder's wallet at the same instant the deliverable is accepted and
 anchored to the ledger. Before acceptance the money is reserved and unspendable ;
 after acceptance the deliverable's hash is on the chain . There is no state in which
 the worker has been paid and no evidence exists, or evidence exists and the escrow is
 still sitting unreleased.

This is delivery-versus-payment with a deliverable in place of a security.

sections.heading: 4. Where the money sits
sections.text:
Escrow reuses the e₹-W wallet already on the rail. No new money primitive, no second
ledger, no chance of the two disagreeing.
 Transition Effect on wallets 
 --- --- 
 fund funder ReservedPaise += fee (requires available = fee ) 
 accept funder Balance -= fee , Reserved -= fee ; worker Balance += fee 
 refund / cancel funder Reserved -= fee 

Two consequences worth stating plainly:

1. Conservation is untouched. Σ wallet balances still equals lifetime funding at every
 point, because escrow only ever reserves, and acceptance is a transfer between two
 wallets. GET /umi/reconciliation keeps proving it.
2. Reserved money cannot be double-spent. The DvP engine computes a buyer's capacity
 from available() , which already subtracts Reserved . Escrowing a repair fee therefore
 reduces what that participant can spend on a settlement, automatically. Nothing in the
 settlement path had to change.

All arithmetic is integer paise. Fees never touch a float.

sections.heading: 5. Evidence on the chain
sections.text:
Each transition appends a block to the existing hash-chained Drunix ledger, so
 /api/chain/verify proves the work history exactly as it proves settlement history:

 WORK CREATED · WORK FUNDED · WORK ASSIGNED · WORK SUBMITTED · WORK ACCEPTED ·
 WORK DISPUTED · WORK REFUNDED · WORK CANCELLED 

 WORK SUBMITTED carries the deliverable's SHA-256 and its URI. That hash is the whole
point: the inspection report handed over in month three can be re-hashed in year five and
checked against a block nobody can rewrite.

Because every transition is on the chain, the work desk restores itself from the ledger
at boot ( RestoreWorkFromChain ). It needs no new database table and no change to
 UMIStore , and it cannot drift from the audit trail, because the audit trail is the
source.

sections.heading: 6. Who may do what
sections.text:
Enforced in Go, next to the state it protects. The JS layer stays a pure proxy.
 Action Permitted caller 
 --- --- 
 create, fund, assign the funder, or a supervisor 
 submit the assigned worker, or a supervisor 
 accept, dispute, refund, cancel the funder, or a supervisor 
 read one order either party, or a supervisor 
 list orders your own (as funder or worker); supervisors see the desk 

Supervisor = role regulator or admin , the same definition the rail already uses.
A worker cannot accept their own work, and a funder cannot submit on the worker's behalf:
that separation is the reason the escrow means anything.

sections.heading: 7. The talent boundary
sections.text:
No external talent provider is configured, so the integration is written as an
adapter with an honest fallback, the same pattern the repo already uses for NPCI:

 

 GET /umi/work/provider reports which mode is active, and every work-order payload carries
 providerMode , so a screenshot can never imply an integration that is not wired up. The request
shape is this project's own, not a vendor's published contract, so pointing it at a real service
means mapping field names inside the adapter. That one file is the only thing that changes, which
is the point of putting the seam there.

What crosses the boundary is deliberately small: publish an order's spec and acceptance
criteria, receive a worker reference back, record it as providerRef . Escrow, state and
evidence stay on our ledger. No external party is asked to hold money, and none is
asking us to host their talent graph.

sections.heading: 9. What this is not
sections.text:
- Not a connection to any real gig-work platform. No such integration exists here, and every
 response says simulation until an endpoint is configured.
- Not an employment or payroll system. It escrows a fee against one defined deliverable.
- Not a dispute court. DISPUTED parks the escrow and names a reason; resolving it is a
 supervisor decision, recorded, not an algorithm pretending to judge.
